papers.selection_reason: Proposes compute-efficient patch selection for byte-level language models, relevant to token-level efficiency and LM architecture.
papers.title: Patch where the text is new: a compression view of where byte-level models should spend compute
papers.tldr: Novelty-based byte patching directs compute toward new content near mathematical computations, substantially improving computed-result and final-answer accuracy under fixed patch budgets.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models expose an inference-time choice: which positions become visible after each denoising pass. Many existing decoding methods use hand-designed rules or require visibility to grow monotonically. We present a $\textbf{T}$iny $\textbf{I}$nference-time $\textbf{P}$olicy for $\textbf{S}$caling ($\textbf{TIPS}$), an approximately $600$K-parameter controller that learns both unmasking and remasking while keeping the underlying language model frozen. TIPS uses visibility-aware confidence features and a shallow transformer to select which tokens should be visible, while a fixed schedule controls the expected visible fraction. We train the controller through supervised warmup followed by reinforcement learning from terminal correctness rewards. On GSM8K and MATH-500 with LLaDA-8B-Instruct, the full-canvas and two-block TIPS variants achieve $58.46\%$ and $57.97\%$ micro-averaged accuracy at a budget of $32$ decoder evaluations, exceeding the strongest baseline in our main comparison by $12.1$ and $11.6$ percentage points, respectively. Both variants are trained at a budget of $32$ evaluations and remain competitive at higher budgets without retraining. These results demonstrate that learning when to reveal and reconsider tokens can improve the accuracy-compute trade-off without updating the decoder backbone.
authors: Ya-Shi Zhang, Jian Tang, Pierre-Andr\'e No\"el, Oleksiy Ostapenko
bullets: Addresses the limitation of hand-designed or monotonically expanding visibility schedules in masked diffusion language models.
Uses visibility-aware confidence features and a shallow transformer to select token visibility, with a fixed schedule controlling the expected visible fraction.
Trains a roughly 600K-parameter controller using supervised warmup followed by reinforcement learning from terminal correctness rewards.

With LLaDA-8B-Instruct at 32 decoder evaluations, TIPS reaches 58.46% and 57.97% micro-averaged accuracy on GSM8K and MATH-500, respectively, outperforming the strongest cited baseline by 12.1 and 11.6 percentage points.
The full-canvas and two-block variants remain competitive at higher inference budgets without retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a small inference-time controller (TIPS) for diffusion language models to optimize the accuracy-compute trade-off by dynamically managing token visibility, directly relevant to LLM memory and long-context management.
papers.title: TIPS: A Tiny Inference-time Policy for Scaling in Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: TIPS is a small learned inference-time controller that improves diffusion language model decoding by deciding which tokens to reveal or remask while keeping the backbone frozen.

papers.abstract: Contrastive vision-language pre-training supports zero-shot chest X-ray diagnosis, but standard objectives treat every off-diagonal image-report pair in a batch as a negative. In radiology, recurring findings across patients mean that instance mismatch need not imply semantic incompatibility, creating false-negative supervision that we term a semantic conflict. A training-trace audit shows that pair-observations selected by the online mask used during training are enriched for report-derived finding agreement, although this proxy analysis does not establish clinical equivalence. Fixed thresholds can become miscalibrated as similarity distributions evolve, while soft reweighting leaves residual repulsive gradients. We therefore propose Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning (SCCL), which tracks modality-specific similarity distributions with exponential-moving-average (EMA) statistics, derives adaptive thresholds, and hard-masks flagged candidates before softmax normalization. Inclusive (OR) and consensus (AND) rules define two SCCL teachers, whose bidirectional cross-modal rankings are consolidated through standard distillation into a single deployable student, SCCL-DT. Across five public chest X-ray benchmarks, SCCL-DT achieves a mean zero-shot AUC of $0.850$, compared with $0.837$ for the strongest evaluated baseline in our comparison. Code will be made publicly available soon.
authors: Ting Liu, Haoran Lai, HaobinChen, Ming Liu, S Kevin Zhou
bullets: Addresses false-negative supervision caused by treating all mismatched image-report pairs as incompatible.
Uses EMA-tracked modality-specific similarity distributions to set adaptive thresholds and hard-mask conflicting candidates before softmax.
Combines inclusive (OR) and consensus (AND) teachers through bidirectional ranking distillation into a deployable student.
Reports mean zero-shot AUC of 0.850 across five public chest X-ray benchmarks, versus 0.837 for the strongest evaluated baseline.
The agreement signal is proxy-based and does not establish clinical equivalence; code is planned for public release.
papers.selection_reason: Contrastive vision-language pretraining with semantic-conflict-aware hard-negative handling; technically transferable to multimodal foundation model alignment.
papers.title: SCCL-DT: Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning with Dual-Rule Teacher Distillation for Zero-Shot Chest X-Ray Diagnosis
papers.tldr: SCCL-DT improves zero-shot chest X-ray diagnosis by identifying and masking semantically conflicting contrastive negatives, then distilling two rule-based teachers into one student.

papers.abstract: Aerial robots operating near people must treat a pedestrian, a parked car, and a wall differently, yet conventional perception--planning stacks reduce all of them to occupied geometry---a \emph{human-aware safety gap} in which category-specific clearance is unavailable to the planner and temporary occlusions remove pedestrian-specific constraints from its map. We present a modular, fully onboard pipeline that closes this gap by turning visual observations into context-dependent safety constraints for real-time UAV navigation. A shared BLIP encoder drives scene captioning and text-conditioned segmentation, which is fused with depth to localize obstacles in 3D. Obstacle-specific risk is inferred by a lightweight LLM (Qwen-2.5-0.5B) stabilized with retrieval-augmented generation and grammar-constrained decoding that restricts its output to a planner-compatible JSON schema. The LLM reasons once per object category rather than per frame: its verdicts are cached per class, so previously seen categories are resolved without inference and new ones trigger a fresh retrieval-grounded query; detections are additionally given persistent identities and held in the map across occlusions. The perception pipeline runs at 10\,Hz on a Jetson Orin NX, while fallback LLM queries take approximately 0.8\,s and remain off the control-critical path. In Gazebo, low-altitude urban navigation among pedestrians and vehicles shows a roughly $3\times$ reduction in collision events over a geometric planner, and semantics-aware landing among moving actors raises success from 34\% to 96\%. The 224-pixel encoder input limits reliable small-object perception at range; conservative pedestrian margins and short-term persistence mitigate this limitation during navigation.
authors: Siwei Cai, Yuwei Wu, Vijay Kumar, Lifeng Zhou
bullets: Addresses the human-aware safety gap: pedestrians, vehicles, and walls receive different clearance requirements instead of being treated as generic occupied geometry.
Fuses BLIP-based captioning and text-conditioned segmentation with depth to localize obstacles in 3D.
Uses a lightweight Qwen-2.5-0.5B LLM with retrieval grounding and grammar-constrained JSON outputs; category-level verdicts are cached and detections persist through occlusions.
Runs perception at 10 Hz on a Jetson Orin NX, with fallback LLM queries kept off the control-critical path.
In Gazebo, collision events decrease by roughly 3×, while semantic landing success among moving actors increases from 34% to 96%; small-object perception at range remains limited.
papers.selection_reason: Onboard LLM-based human-aware safety constraint generation for UAV navigation, fitting learned robot navigation.
papers.title: Onboard Lightweight LLM Reasoning for Human-Aware Safe UAV Navigation
papers.tldr: A fully onboard UAV system uses lightweight vision and LLM-based object reasoning to impose category-specific safety constraints, reducing collisions and improving semantic landing success in simulation.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning datasets remain overwhelmingly English-centric and commercially restricted, as their content is frequently generated by proprietary models whose terms of service forbid training competing systems. We introduce Multi-SFT, a commercially permissive collection of 502,818 instruction-response pairs across five European languages, built via translation and regeneration pipelines for tasks where translation is insufficient. Human evaluation yields inter-annotator agreement of at least 0.87 across all datasets and languages. Fine-tuning nine models from three different families (EuroLLM, OLMo 2, Qwen3; 1B-32B) and evaluating them on 13 benchmarks shows that Multi-SFT alone is competitive with larger augmented mixes and official instruction-tuned releases, with decisive advantages on safety tasks.
authors: Daniela Baiamonte, Kamyar Zeinalipour, Elena Fano, Stefano Simonazzi, Andrea Zugarini
bullets: Addresses the lack of open, commercially usable multilingual supervised fine-tuning data.
Contains 502,818 instruction-response pairs in five European languages.
Uses translation and regeneration pipelines, with regeneration for tasks where direct translation is insufficient.
Human evaluations report inter-annotator agreement of at least 0.87 across datasets and languages.
Fine-tuning nine models across three families and evaluation on 13 benchmarks show competitiveness with larger mixtures and official instruction-tuned releases, with clear safety-task advantages.
papers.selection_reason: Multilingual permissively-licensed instruction-following dataset for SFT; fits LLM instruction tuning.
papers.title: Multi-SFT: Permissively-Licensed Multilingual Instruction-Following
papers.tldr: Multi-SFT is a commercially permissive multilingual instruction-tuning dataset that enables strong performance across five European languages, especially on safety tasks.

papers.abstract: Neural networks offer critical adaptability for controlling complex systems where nominal modeling proves intractable. However, when offline-trained neural networks are deployed within closed-loop control systems, their actions fundamentally alter the state distribution upon which they were trained. This paper introduces a unified taxonomy to categorize these sequential failure modes: the initial Closed-Loop Identification Error, the deployment-induced Action Error, and the continuous Tracking Error. Through discrete-time sensitivity analysis, this work formalizes how offline-learned parameters locally guarantee a trajectory divergence upon deployment, degrading performance due to local loss geometry. To mitigate this distribution shift, we propose actionable design policies centered on time-scale separated online adaptation. These mechanisms are validated through ablation studies on a nonlinear Duffing oscillator, demonstrating that bounded continuous learning successfully mitigates trajectory divergence whereas static deployments fail, offering concrete guidelines for practitioners deploying machine learning components in safety-critical feedback systems.
authors: Vittorio Lippi
bullets: Identifies three sequential failure modes: Closed-Loop Identification Error, deployment-induced Action Error, and continuous Tracking Error.
Uses discrete-time sensitivity analysis to formalize how local loss geometry can cause deployment trajectories to diverge from those seen during training.
Proposes time-scale-separated online adaptation policies to mitigate deployment-induced distribution shift.
Ablations on a nonlinear Duffing oscillator show bounded continuous learning mitigates trajectory divergence, unlike static deployment.
Targets safer deployment of learned control components in safety-critical feedback systems.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes deployment-time distribution shift in closed-loop neural control and proposes online adaptation, fitting test-time and continual learning.
papers.title: Learning Changes the World and Then What Was Learned has Changed: Training and Deploying Neural Networks in the Control Loop
papers.tldr: Offline-trained neural networks can destabilize closed-loop control by changing the data distribution they encounter, while bounded online adaptation helps prevent trajectory divergence.

papers.abstract: Recent work shows that depth recurrence can be retrofitted into pretrained language models. In this work, we adapt this paradigm for visual understanding, using depth recurrence to reduce the parameter footprint of a pretrained vision-language model (VLM). To this end, we prune layers from the language backbone of the VLM and loop over a subset of the remaining layers. At each step of the loop, a linear adapter merges the block's output with the token representations from the preceding layers and projects the fused representation back into the block. As the pruning impacts the original model performance, we propose a three-stage recovery training: first, we leverage a language-only pretraining to recover the performance of the language backbone, followed by an alignment of the vision-language projector, and a full fine-tuning of the model via visual instruction tuning. In the first and the last stage, we distill the outputs of the pretrained non-recurrent model into the recurrent model, which further improves the recovery. We evaluate the proposed approach on the TinyLLaVA-1.4B backbone without introducing any new vision-language data during retrofitting. Our experiments demonstrate that the retrofitted recurrent model outperforms the unpruned baseline trained with the same recovery data while storing 23.3% fewer language parameters. We further show that the proposed retrofitting recurrence outperforms the setup of converting a recurrent LM into a VLM on the same data. Additionally, our ablations show how design choices, such as the adapter between recurrences and a larger recurrent block, lead to the improved performance of our approach. Finally, we find that our proposed model gains on reasoning-oriented benchmarks, whereas its performance on basic visual understanding benchmarks remains on par with the baseline.
authors: Madhav Iyengar, Andreas Geiger, Hilde K\"uhne
bullets: Prunes the language backbone and repeatedly applies a subset of its layers, using linear adapters to merge representations across recurrences.
Uses three-stage recovery: language-backbone training, vision-language projector alignment, and visual instruction tuning.
Distills outputs from the original non-recurrent model during the first and final recovery stages.
On TinyLLaVA-1.4B, the retrofitted model outperforms an equally recovered unpruned baseline without adding vision-language data.
Improvements are strongest on reasoning benchmarks; basic visual understanding remains comparable to the baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces VLM parameters via recurrence, fitting both multimodal foundation models and efficiency.
papers.title: Retrofitting Recurrent Vision-Language Models from Pretrained Backbones
papers.tldr: A pretrained vision-language model can be made recurrent and 23.3% smaller in language parameters while matching or improving performance through structured recovery training and distillation.

papers.abstract: Many hierarchical byte-level language models group bytes into patches using a learned boundary predictor whose view of the next codepoint depends on encoding and lookahead. In UTF-8, codepoints of many scripts take three bytes: 8 of 24 bits mark length and continuation, and the first byte carries only 4 high codepoint bits. After the same left context, a mark extending a grapheme cluster and a letter starting the next can thus share their first byte. Universal Byte-Level Encoding (UBE) keeps one- and two-byte UTF-8 encodings but writes these codepoints as two UTF-16 bytes, low byte first, so its first symbol carries 8 low codepoint bits that can distinguish such continuations. We train small causal predictors on matched FineWeb-2 text and evaluate on FLORES-200 under UTF-8, UBE, and UBE's same-length big-endian variant. At one-symbol lookahead, balanced grapheme-boundary error at codepoint boundaries across 17 languages in 13 Brahmic scripts is 8.76% with UTF-8, 8.62% with the big-endian variant, and 0.06% with UBE. When the target instead retains a parent tokenizer's subword cuts at grapheme boundaries, UBE lowers the mean error relative to UTF-8 at the same lookahead by 72.91% in Korean, 35.29% in Chinese, and 67.32-99.55% in eight more scripts. In the seven of them whose main Unicode block fits on one 256-codepoint page, the big-endian variant stays within 3.0% of UTF-8, so the gain follows byte order, not length. In Korean and Chinese, UBE's mean error falls below UTF-8's final mean error after only 25% and 37.5% of training. Which byte comes first thus affects how much lookahead a byte-level boundary predictor needs.
authors: Hyunsik Kim
bullets: UTF-8 can make a grapheme continuation and a following letter indistinguishable from their first byte in many scripts.
Universal Byte-Level Encoding (UBE) retains short UTF-8 encodings but represents longer codepoints as low-byte-first UTF-16.
Across 17 languages and 13 Brahmic scripts, one-symbol balanced boundary error was 0.06% with UBE versus 8.76% with UTF-8.
For parent-tokenizer subword boundaries, UBE reduced mean error by 35.29–99.55% across the reported scripts, including Korean and Chinese.
The comparison with a big-endian variant indicates that byte order—not encoding length—drives the improvement; scope is focused on boundary prediction and the evaluated multilingual text settings.
papers.selection_reason: Studies byte-level tokenization and boundary prediction for hierarchical language models, relevant to LLM architecture and tokenization.
papers.title: The Right Byte First: How UTF-16 Helps Multilingual Boundary Prediction
papers.tldr: Putting the low UTF-16 byte first substantially improves multilingual grapheme-boundary prediction compared with UTF-8 at the same lookahead.

papers.abstract: Streaming vision-language models (VLMs) must continuously integrate information from the past while remaining responsive to current observations and user queries. Existing memory mechanisms typically compress, retrieve, or cache historical observations and reintroduce them into the input context, forcing historical memory and current observations to compete for limited context. We propose MaLoW, a streaming memory framework that instead internalizes historical context into evolving lightweight parameter updates. MaLoW uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to incrementally consolidate incoming video observations into fixed-size LoRA weights, allowing historical information to be carried forward without revisiting the full video stream. In doing so, MaLoW represents history as weights, while keeping the current observation as input. To support training, we further construct MaLoW-Instruct, a large-scale streaming video dataset containing 381K question-answer pairs over 56K videos. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate that MaLoW achieves strong performance on OVO-Bench, StreamingBench, and StreamArena. On the backward split of OVO-Bench, MaLoW outperforms prior memory approaches by 3.9% to 11.8% across different video backbones while incurring only modest latency overhead. Beyond streaming video understanding, MaLoW also generalizes to vision-language-action models, improving the action success rate on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%.
authors: Zhuoming Liu, Jinhong Lin, Lin Zhang, Yiwu Zhong, Yin Li
bullets: Addresses the context bottleneck caused by memory methods that retrieve or append historical video observations to current inputs.
Uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to consolidate incoming observations into fixed-size LoRA parameter updates while keeping current observations as input.
Introduces MaLoW-Instruct, a streaming-video instruction dataset with 381K question-answer pairs across 56K videos.
Achieves 3.9%–11.8% higher performance than prior memory approaches on OVO-Bench’s backward split, with modest latency overhead.
Also improves action success on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%, suggesting applicability to vision-language-action models.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming VLM memory via LoRA weights; improves video understanding and VLA action success.
papers.title: Memory as Weights: Internalizing Long-Term History for Streaming Videos
papers.tldr: MaLoW turns long-term video history into evolving LoRA weights, enabling streaming VLMs to retain context without repeatedly reloading past observations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can act unsafely when individually benign images and texts are interpreted jointly. Beyond implicit reasoning risk, where reasoning drifts toward harm, we identify intent-level risk, where cross-modal ambiguity silently commits the model to a hazardous premise that path-level optimization alone cannot correct. We propose SAFE-PRO, which uses a Risk-Conditioned Uncertainty (RCU) signal, combining predictive entropy with a learned cross-modal risk score, to decide when to ask safety-grounded clarifying questions and where to apply path optimization, under a reward that prioritizes safety and penalizes over-refusal. We also build SSUI-Dialog, a multimodal multi-turn dataset with dual-intent supervision, and theoretically analyze gradient variance and unsafe-completion risk under RCU. Across seven benchmarks and two base MLLMs, SAFE-PRO consistently improves safety over SRPO, roughly halves its over-refusal, and surpasses GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet in average single-turn safety.
authors: Wei Cai, Jian Zhao, Yuchen Yuan, Xuelong Li
bullets: Identifies intent-level risk: benign images and text can jointly imply hazardous premises that ordinary reasoning optimization may miss.
Uses Risk-Conditioned Uncertainty to trigger safety-grounded clarification and guide path optimization.
Introduces SSUI-Dialog, a multimodal multi-turn dataset with dual-intent supervision.
Theoretically analyzes RCU’s effects on gradient variance and unsafe-completion risk.
Across seven benchmarks and two base MLLMs, improves safety over SRPO, roughly halves over-refusal, and exceeds GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet in average single-turn safety.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses cross-modal safety in multimodal LLMs with proactive inquiry and uncertainty-based routing.
papers.title: When Reasoning Is Not Enough: Proactive Inquiry for Cross-Modal Safety in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: SAFE-PRO improves cross-modal safety in multimodal LLMs by asking targeted clarifying questions when uncertainty and hidden intent-level risk are high.

papers.abstract: Long-context language models support ever longer context windows, and evaluations typically treat context length as the main indicator of difficulty. However, context length alone cannot explain why models fail on long-context tasks that require reasoning over complex information. Contexts of equal length can pose very different challenges: a task may be solvable from a single local passage, or it may require integrating evidence distributed across the full context. We quantitatively characterise this difficulty through three properties: evidence scope, how much necessary information must be found; evidence dispersion, how widely that information is scattered within the context; and reasoning depth, how many dependent steps are needed to derive an answer from it. We construct LURCH, a multi-domain question-answering benchmark of 6,550 instances with supporting evidence and reasoning graphs, enabling all three properties to be quantified. Evaluations of proprietary and open-weight models show that: (1) at fixed context length, all our three properties are strongly negatively correlated with model performance; (2) as context length increases, performance degrades sharply on samples with dispersed evidence, whereas it remains relatively stable on samples with localised evidence; and (3) difficulty compounds across properties, as questions with moderately high values on all three are harder than those with an extreme value on just one. These findings establish evidence scope, dispersion and reasoning depth as measures of long-context reasoning difficulty that complement context length.
authors: Shiwen Qin, Cameron Barker, Henry Gouk, Elliot J. Crowley, Shay B. Cohen, Mirella Lapata, Miao Li
bullets: Introduces three difficulty dimensions: evidence scope, evidence dispersion, and reasoning depth.
Presents LURCH, a 6,550-instance, multi-domain QA benchmark with supporting evidence and reasoning graphs.
Across proprietary and open-weight models, all three dimensions negatively correlate with performance at fixed context length.
Performance degrades more sharply with increasing context length when evidence is dispersed rather than localized.
Difficulty compounds when moderately high scope, dispersion, and reasoning depth occur together.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses long-context reasoning difficulty with new difficulty measures and a benchmark.
papers.title: Beyond Context Length: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning
papers.tldr: Long-context reasoning difficulty depends not just on context length, but on how much evidence must be found, how dispersed it is, and how many reasoning steps connect it.

papers.abstract: Given a state and a set of options, such as intents, tools or interface elements, System One decision models return a distribution over the options in one forward pass, without generated reasoning. Web systems increasingly build them by reading decisions from language models. Two axioms of rational choice are natural requirements for such decisions, because in web systems the listing and the option set are determined by other components and can change or be manipulated: the order in which the options are listed should not matter, and adding an option should not change the relative odds of the others (Luce's choice axiom). We test the standard reads, namely single-choice question (SCQ) prompting, with shuffled-order training, order averaging or sorted options, and invariant set architectures, and find that each violates at least one axiom: one shuffle changes 12-20% of SCQ answers, sorting only freezes an arbitrary convention, and a well-chosen added option steers 4-34% of decisions. By Luce's theorem, a read satisfies both axioms only if it is a softmax over scores that each depend on one option alone, so in a transformer they hold by construction only if no token that scores an option sees another. We implement this as Prism-1 (Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models): every option is read in its own block at shared positions, with the model's usual left-to-right attention, in one forward pass. On five benchmark sets with Qwen3-8B and Gemma 4 12B, SCQ prompting trained on the same data still changes 7% of its answers under one shuffle, and an added irrelevant option steers 12% of its decisions. Prism-1 stays within one point of that baseline's accuracy and is 2-4 points more accurate once only answers that survive a reordering are counted, while no shuffle changes any of its answers and no added irrelevant option moves its choice among the others.
authors: Yao Long Teng, Jianguo Huang, Yanchen Deng, Jiayi Cai, Bo An
bullets: Web System One models should be insensitive to option order and to adding competing options, as required by rational-choice axioms.
Standard SCQ prompting, even with shuffling, sorting, or invariant architectures, violates at least one axiom.
Prism-1 scores each option independently in separate blocks at shared positions, using one forward pass.
Across five benchmark sets with Qwen3-8B and Gemma 4 12B, Prism-1 had no changes under shuffling or irrelevant-option additions.
Its accuracy stayed within one point of the baseline and was 2–4 points higher when counting only reorder-stable answers.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a novel LLM scoring architecture satisfying rational-choice axioms, relevant to LLM architectural advances.
papers.title: Prism-1: Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models
papers.tldr: Prism-1 enforces order- and rival-independent option scoring, eliminating choice changes caused by option reordering or irrelevant additions while preserving baseline accuracy.

papers.abstract: Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms face significant limitations in handling long-term tasks with sparse rewards. Recent advancements have leveraged large language models (LLMs) to enhance RL by utilizing their world knowledge for task planning and reward generation. However, planning-based approaches often depend on pre-defined skill libraries and fail to optimize low-level control policies, while reward-based methods require extensive human feedback or exhaustive searching due to the complexity of tasks. In this paper, we propose the Progress Reward Model for RL (PRM4RL), a novel framework that integrates task planning and dense reward to enhance RL. For high-level planning, a complex task is decomposed into a series of simple manageable subtasks, with a subtask-oriented, fine-grained progress function designed to monitor task execution progress. For low-level reward generation, inspired by potential-based reward shaping, we use the progress function to construct a Progress Reward Model (PRM), providing theoretically grounded optimality and convergence guarantees, thereby enabling effective policy optimization. Experimental results on robotics control tasks demonstrate that our approach outperforms both LLM-based planning and reward methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/deng-ai-lab/PRM4RL.
authors: Xiuhui Zhang, Ning Gao, Xingyu Jiang, Yihui Chen, Yuheng Pan, Mohan Zhang, Yue Deng
bullets: Addresses sparse rewards and the difficulty of learning long-term tasks with conventional RL.
Decomposes complex tasks into manageable subtasks and monitors fine-grained execution progress.
Uses a progress function to construct dense rewards inspired by potential-based reward shaping.
Provides theoretical optimality and convergence guarantees for policy optimization.
Outperforms existing LLM-based planning and reward methods on robotics control tasks, according to the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Uses LLM-based planning and progress rewards to improve reinforcement learning for robotics control.
papers.title: Progress Reward Model for Reinforcement Learning via Large Language Models
papers.tldr: PRM4RL combines LLM-based task decomposition with theoretically grounded progress rewards to improve reinforcement learning for long-horizon, sparse-reward robotics tasks.

papers.abstract: World-model planners evaluate candidate trajectories by predicting their future consequences, implicitly relying on the plan-to-motion relationship learned during training. At deployment, a different downstream controller may execute the same planned trajectory differently, creating a planning-execution gap between the frozen model's imagined future and actual execution. A natural remedy is to replace the planned trajectory with its predicted or observed execution. However, we find that better execution fidelity does not necessarily yield better decisions: directly substituting predicted execution trajectories yields only a 0.048 PDMS improvement across 10 unseen controller configurations, far smaller than the gain from our proposed adaptation. This suggests a semantic mismatch between a planned trajectory, which serves as a reference for downstream control, and an executed trajectory, which already describes the resulting post-controller motion. We introduce ExecutionBridge, which infers controller-specific execution characteristics from planned-executed trajectory pairs and uses them to adapt the native ego latent rollout while keeping the original planned trajectory unchanged. The planner, world model, and reward head remain frozen. On NAVSIM, ExecutionBridge consistently improves planning across unseen controller configurations and multiple frozen world-model planners, with substantially larger gains in challenging driving scenes where execution mismatch more strongly affects candidate evaluation.
authors: Danqi Zhao, Keyu Chen, Wenchao Sun, Minglei Huang, Jianhe Zhang, Yan Zhu, Hao Cheng, Zifan Cao, Sifa Zheng
bullets: Problem: Different downstream controllers can execute the same plan differently, causing a gap between imagined and actual outcomes.
Naively substituting predicted or observed execution trajectories improves fidelity but does not reliably improve planning decisions.
Method: Infer controller-specific execution characteristics from planned–executed trajectory pairs and adapt the planner’s native ego latent rollout.
The world model, planner, and reward head remain frozen; the original planned trajectory is preserved.
On NAVSIM, the method consistently improves planning across unseen controllers and multiple frozen planners, especially in challenging driving scenes.
papers.selection_reason: Adapts frozen world-model planners to controller-induced execution shift for navigation, directly relevant to robot planning and world models.
papers.title: Plans Are Not Executions: Adapting Frozen World-Model Planners to Controller-Induced Execution Shift
papers.tldr: ExecutionBridge adapts frozen world-model planners to controller-specific motion without replacing the original plan, improving decisions under unseen execution behaviors.

papers.abstract: Current heterogeneity-aware training systems for large models balance workloads by assigning unequal numbers of layers across pipeline stages, a strategy aimed at equalizing execution time through a unique pipeline configuration. However, this approach fails to address critical memory constraints and suffers from inherently coarse balancing granularity. In this paper, we propose Heterogeneous Pipeline Parallelism (HPP), a novel approach enabling efficient and fine-grained data balance across heterogeneous pipelines. To address HPP's key challenges, prohibitive search overhead for optimal configurations and high communication overhead from asymmetric All-Reduce, we design the ETH training system. ETH employs a hierarchical workload balance framework that jointly optimizes balance across heterogeneous pipelines and within individual pipeline stages. To mitigate asymmetric communication costs, ETH implements block-wise gradient aggregation. Furthermore, it integrates specialized optimizations that dramatically reduce HPP configuration search overhead. Evaluations demonstrate ETH achieves up to 2x training speedup while reducing configuration generation overhead by up to 56x compared to state-of-the-art systems. The code is available at https://github.com/YuMJie/ETH.
authors: Mianjie Yu, Zhongmin Zhao, Zizhao Mo, Jianxiong Liao, Wenxuan Li, Yulin Qiao, Huanle Xu, Wenquan Yang, Yongqiang Yang, Zeren Li, Ruifeng Tang, Chengzhong Xu
bullets: Existing heterogeneous pipeline methods use coarse layer-count balancing and may not satisfy memory constraints.
ETH introduces Heterogeneous Pipeline Parallelism for data balance across and within heterogeneous pipelines.
A hierarchical balancing framework jointly optimizes inter-pipeline and intra-stage workloads.
Block-wise gradient aggregation reduces communication costs from asymmetric All-Reduce.
Evaluations report up to 2× training speedup and 56× lower configuration-generation overhead versus prior systems.
papers.selection_reason: Heterogeneous pipeline parallelism for large-model training reduces training time and configuration overhead, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: ETH: Data-Balanced Heterogeneous Pipeline Parallelism for Training Large Models
papers.tldr: ETH enables fine-grained workload balancing across heterogeneous pipeline configurations, achieving up to 2× faster large-model training with up to 56× lower configuration-generation overhead.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving language models train on tasks they generate, so every round must decide which updated model the next round inherits. Current loops such as R-Zero, Agent0, and Skill Self-Play make this decision through the task, admitting tasks that look learnable and inheriting every resulting update. We identify a selection-to-update gap in these loops, where a task that looks learnable need not produce a useful update. Most updates on verified tasks fail to make correct answers more likely, yet these loops inherit them all. HeirCommit freezes the updated model and uses fresh evaluation questions to decide whether to inherit it or retain the current model. EvoHeir separates parameter inheritance from experience inheritance, using current and archived experience to repair failures and preserve successes before final confirmation. Our analysis characterizes selection-induced optimism and decomposes regret into selection, absorption, and confirmation errors. HeirCommit cuts the harmful share of accepted updates by 68-83% relative to random inheritance at the same acceptance rate. Across four backbones, EvoHeir achieves the best mathematics and general-reasoning averages, raising the math average by 5.3% relative to the strongest baseline, Agent0. The framework lets useful experience persist even when the model that produced it is not inherited.
authors: Haoyi Yang, Kshitij Mishra, Nils Lukas, Salem Lahlou
bullets: Self-evolving loops often inherit updates from tasks that appear learnable, even when those updates do not improve correctness.
HeirCommit evaluates frozen candidate models on fresh questions before deciding whether to inherit them.
EvoHeir separates parameter inheritance from experience inheritance, allowing useful experience to persist despite rejecting its originating model.
The analysis decomposes regret into selection, absorption, and confirmation errors and characterizes selection-induced optimism.
HeirCommit reduces harmful accepted updates by 68–83%; EvoHeir obtains the best reported mathematics and general-reasoning averages across four backbones.
papers.selection_reason: Selection mechanisms for self-evolving LLM training loops; fits LLM training methodology.
papers.title: Selection Is Not Learning: Choosing Model Futures
papers.tldr: HeirCommit and EvoHeir improve self-evolving language-model training by verifying whether updates are useful before inheritance and preserving valuable experience independently of model selection.

papers.abstract: Learning from demonstration is an effective strategy for endowing robots with manipulation capabilities but requires training on datasets comprised of massive amounts of demonstrations. Existing demonstration collection approaches either require constant human involvement, for example, via teleoperation or are specialized for a single task. Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) systems are able to autonomously solve and therefore generate demonstrations for general-purpose tasks; however, learning from their demonstrations has proven difficult due to multi-modality in their solutions. In this work, we build on recent work leveraging GPU acceleration for TAMP and propose DemoStream, a TAMP system that optimizes demonstration quality in order to improve behavior cloning success rates. First, we introduce batched TAMP sampling operations along with a new TAMP algorithm that correspondingly performs batched constraint satisfaction in order to explore many solutions in parallel. We conduct simulation experiments ablating different action spaces, cost functions, and batch sizes to analyze the effect of these choices on downstream policy success rates. Finally, we show that we can leverage the safety guarantees of TAMP to directly collect real-world demonstrations at an average rate of 66 demos per hour. See our website for policy rollout videos: demostream.github.io.
authors: Caelan Garrett, Neel Jawale, Fabio Ramos
bullets: Addresses the need for scalable, autonomous demonstration collection beyond teleoperation or task-specific systems.
Introduces batched TAMP sampling and batched constraint satisfaction to explore many solutions in parallel.
Optimizes demonstration quality to mitigate multimodal solutions and improve behavior-cloning success rates.
Evaluates action spaces, cost functions, and batch sizes in simulation, and collects real-world demonstrations at an average of 66 per hour.
Scope: Results are presented through simulation ablations and a real-world demonstration-collection demonstration; the abstract does not specify broader task coverage or policy performance details.
papers.selection_reason: TAMP-based automated demonstration collection for robot manipulation learning; fits robot learning.
papers.title: DemoStream: Batched Task-and-Motion-Plan Optimization for Automated Learning from Demonstration
papers.tldr: DemoStream uses batched GPU-accelerated task-and-motion planning to generate higher-quality, diverse demonstrations for more effective robot behavior cloning.

papers.abstract: Frontier models, general-purpose and domain-specific alike, now include a midtraining stage between pretraining and post-training, but little has been published about how this stage is built. We present an open midtraining recipe that primes base models for agentic post-training, and we show its effectiveness on two Nemotron models of different sizes. Pretraining typically runs at short context and sees almost no agent interactions, while SFT data is mostly synthetic, and very long SFT stages can hurt the model's later RL trainability. Our midtraining stage sits between the two. It trains at 256K context for hundreds of billions of tokens on a diverse mixture of natural software-engineering data like packed repositories, pull requests, commit histories, and build logs together with a small share of agentic traces. On Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, 500B midtraining tokens improve SWE-bench Verified from 60.7 to 64.5, SWE-bench Multilingual from 55.8 to 62.8, and SWE-bench Pro from 32.0 to 35.5 after identical full SFT. On the larger Nemotron 3.5 Super, 280B midtraining tokens improve DeepSWE, a harder benchmark of long-horizon tasks, from 11.7 to 15.7 and SWE-bench Verified from 72.9 to 74.3 after identical full SFT. Midtraining also improves robustness across agent harnesses on both models. We report the ablations behind the recipe and an evaluation protocol built on short fixed SFT runs, since base-model proxy metrics did not correlate reliably with post-training results.
authors: Soumye Singhal, Joseph Jennings, Ka Shun Shum, Alexander Bukharin, Khushi Bhardwaj, Zirui Liu, Venkat Srinivasan, Jonathan Li, Yash Jain, Kezhi Kong, Markus Kliegl, Olivier Delalleau, Sanjeev Satheesh, Mostofa Patwary
bullets: Addresses the underexplored midtraining stage between pretraining and post-training, where short-context pretraining and synthetic-heavy SFT may limit agentic capabilities.
Trains at 256K context on hundreds of billions of tokens from repositories, pull requests, commit histories, build logs, and a small amount of agent traces.
After identical SFT, gains appear across SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-bench Pro, and the long-horizon DeepSWE benchmark on two Nemotron models.
The recipe also improves robustness across agent harnesses.
Proxy metrics from base models were unreliable; the authors instead use short fixed SFT runs and report supporting ablations.
papers.selection_reason: Open midtraining recipe for agentic post-training of LLMs at 256K context; fits LLM training and long-context.
papers.title: Priming Base Models for Agentic Post-Training: An Open Midtraining Recipe
papers.tldr: An open midtraining recipe using long-context software-engineering data and limited agent traces improves models’ subsequent agentic post-training performance and robustness.

papers.abstract: Arabic calligraphy is a high-stakes cultural visual domain for Muslim communities, yet VLM evaluations rarely test its fine-grained script traditions. We audit 12 VLMs on a cleaned 1,195-image six-way benchmark using numeric, visual-cue, and Diwani-first prompts. In this closed-set setting, the best numeric-prompt accuracy is 60.9% for closed/API models and 47.2% for open-weight models. The main failure is default-label collapse: every numeric run is dominated by a single label taking 33-63% of predictions, against an 18.8% majority-class baseline. For 8 of 12 models the default is Thuluth; GPT-4o labels 52.9% of all images as Thuluth although it is only 18.1% of the set. Prompting helps unevenly: visual cues move accuracy by more than 10 points for some models but hurt others, and foregrounding Diwani often relocates the default rather than removing it. Arabic calligraphy recognition is therefore a compact, culturally grounded stress test for VLM robustness and for measuring which visual traditions become legible to automated systems.
authors: Niaz Mohaiman Abtahi, Evan Maksud, Reyana Shahid
bullets: The audit evaluates 12 VLMs on a cleaned 1,195-image, six-way Arabic calligraphy benchmark.
Best numeric-prompt accuracy reaches 60.9% for closed/API models and 47.2% for open-weight models.
All numeric-prompt runs show default-label collapse, with one label receiving 33–63% of predictions versus an 18.8% majority-class baseline.
Prompt strategies have inconsistent effects: visual cues help some models by over 10 points but hurt others, while Diwani-first prompts often shift rather than eliminate the default.
The benchmark serves as a culturally grounded stress test for VLM robustness and the visual traditions recognized by automated systems.
papers.selection_reason: Audits VLMs for calligraphy recognition, fits MLLM evaluation.
papers.title: When Models Misread Ink: Auditing VLMs for Arabic Calligraphy Recognition
papers.tldr: VLMs struggle to reliably distinguish Arabic calligraphy styles, often collapsing predictions onto a culturally prominent default label.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used to interpret religious, educational, and culturally sensitive visual content, yet their reliability on citation verification remains underexplored. We introduce Visual Sanad, a controlled benchmark for testing whether VLMs falsely accept incorrect Qur'anic verse attributions when the same quote-reference pair is rendered under different visual framings. The benchmark contains 2,400 rendered images built from 100 English Qur'an verses, four factual states per verse, and six visual conditions ranging from plain text to decorative and authority-framed layouts. All quote-reference pairs were source-checked and human-audited before rendering. Across 24 full model-prompt runs, we observe a sharp capability split. Proprietary API-served VLMs range from near-perfect citation verification to moderate false acceptance, whereas recent open-weight VLMs often show weak discrimination and default to VALID on most images. De-biased prompting can reduce false acceptance, but often by shifting the decision threshold toward INVALID rather than by producing strong citation discrimination. Visual Sanad therefore exposes a culturally grounded multimodal factuality failure: fluent VLMs may treat displayed religious citations as self-authenticating unless they have strong citation-verification ability.
authors: Niaz Mohaiman Abtahi, Reyana Shahid, Evan Maksud
bullets: Introduces a controlled benchmark of 2,400 rendered images based on 100 English Qur'an verses and four factual states.
Tests citation verification across six visual framings, from plain text to decorative and authority-framed layouts.
Finds a sharp capability split: proprietary VLMs range from near-perfect verification to moderate false acceptance, while many open-weight models default to VALID.
De-biased prompting can lower false acceptance but may simply shift models toward INVALID rather than improve discrimination.
Highlights a culturally sensitive multimodal factuality failure: displayed citations may be treated as self-authenticating.
papers.selection_reason: Audits VLMs for citation verification, fits MLLM evaluation.
papers.title: Visual Sanad: Auditing Vision-Language Models for False Acceptance of Qur'anic Citations
papers.tldr: Visual Sanad shows that vision-language models may falsely accept incorrect Qur'anic citations, especially when visual design conveys authority.

papers.abstract: Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT) is an essential capability for intelligent robots in human-robot collaboration, requiring an agent to follow a designated target person in dynamic environments relying solely on egocentric visual perception. However, persistent pedestrian occlusions in dynamic scenes pose critical challenges to existing EVT methods. Lacking proactive visibility preservation, reactive tracking methods frequently experience prolonged target loss under severe occlusions. Therefore, we propose VP-EVT, a framework that treats target visibility as an explicit objective of motion control rather than a by-product of following. Acting on this objective requires understanding both what obstructs the target and how robot motion can change that obstruction. VP-EVT therefore uses language-guided perception to extract separate target and pedestrian observations. When occlusion makes current observations incomplete, VP-EVT combines visual history with ego-motion to maintain estimates of their relative positions and motion. Using these estimates and the current following waypoints, VP-EVT predicts whether continued following will sustain the obstruction. When the predicted risk is low, the original following motion is retained; otherwise, a recurrent controller combines updated estimates with maneuver context from preceding decisions to coordinate viewpoint adjustment and the return to stable following. Moreover, we introduce OccEVT-Bench for closed-loop evaluation of persistent occlusion and collect expert demonstrations for training. On its Risk split, VP-EVT improves success rate by 121.4% relative to a competitive baseline and reduces visibility deficit and longest target-loss duration by 78.8% and 74.4%, respectively.
authors: Yanci Wen, Tianle Zeng, Jianwei Peng, Weixi Situ, Hanjing Ye, Hong Zhang
bullets: Addresses prolonged target loss caused by pedestrian occlusions in dynamic environments.
Uses language-guided perception to separate target and occluder observations, then combines visual history with ego-motion to estimate relative motion during partial visibility.
Predicts whether continued following will maintain occlusion and selectively triggers viewpoint-adjustment maneuvers through a recurrent controller.
Introduces OccEVT-Bench and expert demonstrations for closed-loop evaluation and training.
On the Risk split, improves success rate by 121.4% and reduces visibility deficit and longest target-loss duration by 78.8% and 74.4%.
papers.selection_reason: Embodied visual tracking with proactive visibility preservation, using ego-motion history and recurrent control for target following.
papers.title: VP-EVT: Active Visibility Preservation for Embodied Visual Tracking
papers.tldr: VP-EVT enables embodied visual trackers to proactively avoid persistent occlusions by adjusting the robot’s viewpoint while maintaining target following.

papers.abstract: Flow-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are inherently stochastic: different noise seeds can produce action chunks of varying quality from the same observation. At test time, however, the policy typically commits to a single sample without an explicit estimate of its quality. In fine-grained manipulation, executing a suboptimal action can irreversibly disrupt task progress and lead to failure. To exploit policy stochasticity, we introduce a training-free two-axis trigger that uses two initial samples to measure within-chunk temporal variation and cross-sample variance, detecting the critical states. Once triggered, a JEPA-based latent world model ranks candidate action chunks by predicting action-conditioned future latent states and the corresponding changes in task progress. By operating in latent space, the verifier avoids pixel reconstruction and enables efficient and more accurate ranking. Across three real-world tasks, $\textit{i.e.,}$ pen insertion, pipetting, and apple placement), our method raises the average completion score from 50.8% to 65.5%, while adding 326 ms for sampling and verification per triggered decision on a single RTX 4090. Consistent gains are also observed in simulation, where the average success rate rises from 66.4% to 73.6% in the clean setting of RoboTwin 2.0, from 62.8% to 69.6% in its randomized setting, and from 96.9% to 97.6% on LIBERO.
authors: Xueli Sun, Yuxiang Lu, Yantong Liu, Xianzhe Fan, Xi Chen, Zhe Liu, Hengshuang Zhao
bullets: Addresses failures caused by committing to a poor action sample during fine-grained manipulation.
Uses two initial samples to detect critical states from within-chunk temporal variation and cross-sample variance.
When triggered, a JEPA-based latent world model ranks candidate action chunks by predicted future latent states and task-progress changes.
Improves average real-world completion from 50.8% to 65.5% across pen insertion, pipetting, and apple placement, with 326 ms added per triggered decision.
Also reports consistent simulation gains across RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO; verification is applied selectively rather than at every decision.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time verification of flow-based VLA policies using a latent world model to rank action chunks.
papers.title: VeriVLA: Adaptive Test-Time Verification for Flow-Based VLAs with Latent World Models
papers.tldr: VeriVLA improves stochastic flow-based VLA decisions by triggering test-time verification and selecting action chunks with a latent world model.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving planning requires selecting trajectories that remain safe, rule-compliant, and comfortable under complex multi-agent interactions, yet robust closed-loop decision making in planning-critical scenes remains challenging. Existing diffusion- and RL-based planners often rely on generic rewards and use relational structure mainly for representation, limiting how planning-critical rollouts shape policy improvement. We present GRID-Planner, a graph--reward integrated diffusion planning framework that aligns generative planning with structured relational signals. Specifically, GRID-Planner combines graph-aware importance weighting, a time-indexed relational reward surrogate, and an advantage-weighted diffusion objective with on-policy self-distillation, forming a rollout-return-advantage-update loop without explicit likelihoods. Experiments on nuPlan and interPlan show that, compared with the diffusion-only baseline, GRID-Planner reduces collision rate, lane deviation, and jerk by 35.8\%, 60.8\%, and 27.4\%, respectively, and improves the planning score by 3.4\%. Project website: https://github.com/yangzhaojason/GRID-Planner.
authors: Zhao Yang, Zezhong Qian, Yinan Shi, Longjun Liu, Yawei Jueluo
bullets: Targets safer, rule-compliant, and more comfortable planning in complex multi-agent scenes.
Combines graph-aware importance weighting, time-indexed relational reward surrogates, and advantage-weighted diffusion training.
Uses on-policy self-distillation to form a rollout–return–advantage–update loop without explicit likelihoods.
On nuPlan and interPlan, reduces collision rate, lane deviation, and jerk by 35.8%, 60.8%, and 27.4%, respectively, while improving planning score by 3.4% over a diffusion-only baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Graph-structured reward shaping for diffusion planning in autonomous driving.
papers.title: GRID-Planner: Graph-Structured Relational Reward Shaping for Diffusion Planning
papers.tldr: GRID-Planner improves diffusion-based autonomous-driving planning by integrating graph-structured relational rewards with advantage-weighted, on-policy learning.

papers.abstract: Learning from experience requires recovering reusable knowledge and determining when it applies to a new situation. We introduce OntoAct, a hypothesis-based neuro-symbolic framework built on ontological abstraction. OntoAct turns individual experiences into axioms over entity types, relations, and conditions, making their underlying patterns reusable across situations. A large language model (LLM) uses this world knowledge to propose hypotheses and actions, while a symbolic verifier assesses their supporting conditions against current observations. Verification identifies missing evidence, and new observations and intervention outcomes update hypothesis assessments and guide subsequent actions. We also introduce Tacit-FLE, a benchmark built on the Factorio Learning Environment (FLE) for diagnosing and repairing hidden faults in existing factories using inherited operational records. Its synthetic maintenance corpus distributes evidence across records, and an executed repair may leave the fault unresolved, requiring agents to reassess their diagnoses through interaction. Across Tacit-FLE, Mars, and ALFWorld, OntoAct achieves leading task performance with efficient interaction and inference.
authors: Donghyeok Lee, Bong Gyun Kang, Junyong Ahn, Sungroh Yoon
bullets: Represents experiences as reusable axioms over entity types, relations, and conditions.
Uses an LLM to propose hypotheses and actions, while a symbolic verifier checks them against observations.
Identifies missing evidence and updates hypothesis assessments using new observations and intervention outcomes.
Introduces Tacit-FLE, a benchmark for diagnosing and repairing hidden factory faults from distributed operational records.
Reports leading task performance with efficient interaction and inference across Tacit-FLE, Mars, and ALFWorld.
papers.selection_reason: Hypothesis-based neuro-symbolic agent acting in embodied environments fits embodied AI.
papers.title: OntoAct: Hypothesis-Based Neuro-Symbolic Agents through Ontological Abstraction
papers.tldr: OntoAct combines LLM-generated hypotheses with symbolic verification and ontological abstractions to learn reusable knowledge and act effectively under changing evidence.

papers.abstract: Biological visual navigation achieves remarkable robustness at extremely low power, whereas frame-based robotic systems relying on artificial neural networks remain limited in both respects, particularly for energy-constrained micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) operating in complex environments. Inspired by the event-driven, sparse, and asynchronous principles of biological visual systems, neuromorphic sensing and computation provide a promising alternative for robust and energy-efficient navigation. In this paper, we propose the first end-to-end event-driven neuromorphic paradigm for MAV visual navigation in complex environments by integrating neuromorphic vision, spiking neural networks, and neuromorphic processors. The proposed method first extracts the environmental representation from event streams using a spiking perceptual representation module. This representation is fed into a spiking navigation module, where guidance learning and population coding enable efficient policy learning with few time steps. The navigation module then outputs a waypoint converted into executable trajectory points. Experiments show that the proposed neuromorphic method achieves navigation performance comparable to ANN-based methods while markedly reducing power consumption. The spiking perceptual module consumes only 19.57% of the power of its ANN counterpart, while the spiking navigation module deployed on Intel Loihi consumes only 12.37% of that required by its ANN counterpart running on NVIDIA Orin NX. Beyond prior neuromorphic systems focused mainly on relatively simple navigation subtasks, we demonstrate a complete neuromorphic visual navigation system spanning simulation and real-world deployment. Our results establish the feasibility of the neuromorphic paradigm for autonomous navigation and provide a bio-inspired pathway toward robust and low-power MAV navigation.
authors: Junjie Jiang, Ankang Zhou, Zheng Fang
bullets: Targets robust, energy-efficient navigation for micro aerial vehicles in complex environments.
Combines neuromorphic vision, spiking neural networks, and neuromorphic processors.
Uses spiking perceptual representations, guidance learning, and population coding to produce executable waypoints.
Reports power use of 19.57% for the spiking perceptual module and 12.37% for the Loihi-based spiking navigation module relative to ANN counterparts.
Demonstrates a complete system in simulation and real-world deployment, extending beyond simpler neuromorphic navigation subtasks.
papers.selection_reason: Neuromorphic spiking visual navigation for MAVs with waypoint-based policy learning, directly relevant to robot navigation.
papers.title: Towards bio-inspired visual navigation: a neuromorphic navigation paradigm for MAVs
papers.tldr: An end-to-end event-driven neuromorphic system enables MAV visual navigation with ANN-comparable performance and substantially lower power consumption.

papers.abstract: Deepfake detectors safeguard against misinformation, rendering their failures as much a societal as a technical concern. As generators constantly evolve, detectors trained on static datasets miss newly arising threats, while progressive training interferes catastrophically. Yet, mitigating forgetfulness in terms of accuracy, the prevalent focus of continual learning (CL), is insufficient to reflect real-world impact. We therefore scrutinize the effects of CL methods with respect to evolving fairness. To this end, we analyze four dimensions of fairness across diverse demographics for detectors trained progressively on a chronological sequence of 11 real-world deepfake generation methods. Tracking fairness metrics over time, we expose non-trivial interplays between performance and fairness that depend on both the choice of CL algorithm and demographic intersections. We find accuracy degradation to typically exacerbate unfairness and, conversely, fairness improvements to remain scarce over time. Dissecting the CL method families (rehearsal, prompts, regularization), we observe that inequitable forgetting is not explained by underrepresentation alone, but likely entangled with representation learning. We thus issue a call to action for CL methods to take social outcomes into account when balancing the stability-plasticity tradeoff.
authors: Kajaree Das, Oliver B\"ose, Subarnaduti Paul, Gabriel Storch, Martin Mundt
bullets: Studies four fairness dimensions across diverse demographic groups.
Evaluates detectors progressively on 11 chronological, real-world deepfake generation methods.
Finds that accuracy degradation typically worsens unfairness, while fairness improvements are rare over time.
Fairness outcomes vary by continual-learning algorithm and demographic intersection.
Inequitable forgetting is not explained by underrepresentation alone and may involve representation learning.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes fairness of continual learning methods for deepfake detection; fits continual/online learning.
papers.title: Time to Fake It: Continual Machine Learning Intensifies Unfairness in Deepfake Detection
papers.tldr: Continual learning can make deepfake detectors increasingly unfair as they adapt to evolving generation methods, so fairness must be treated alongside accuracy.

papers.abstract: As multimodal AI systems are becoming our everyday thought partners, the shift towards studying how users transfer control to these systems becomes especially urgent. In this paper, we report an overview of findings from an online study with n=56 AI-literate participants and 392 Video Question Answering trials. After inspecting each multimodal AI response, participants rated task-specific trust and selected one of three intended policies for an analogous future task: reject AI assistance, use it with verification, or delegate fully to the AI. Within participants, post-interaction trust strongly predicted the user's delegation choices (OR=14.97, 95% CI [7.14,31.37]). Trust and delegation nevertheless remained distinct. Verification was the dominant policy and often co-occurred with high trust. Delegation also increased with task order after adjustment for momentary and participant-level trust (OR=1.22, 95% CI [1.02,1.45]), indicating an experience-related component that self-reported trust ratings alone could not capture. These findings motivate a shift from intended delegation to a non-intrusive observation of how delegation is enacted in collaborative human-AI tasks. We therefore conclude by proposing enacted delegation traces as a methodological framework for future studies of multimodal and agentic AI use.
authors: Agnese Chiatti, Matteo Matteucci, Viola Schiaffonati
bullets: Studied 56 AI-literate participants across 392 video question-answering trials.
After each response, participants rated task-specific trust and chose to reject, verify, or fully delegate to AI.
Higher post-interaction trust strongly predicted delegation, but trust and delegation were not equivalent.
Verification was the most common policy and often occurred alongside high trust.
Delegation increased with task order, motivating enacted delegation traces as a framework for studying human-AI oversight.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates human delegation and trust in interaction with multimodal AI (Video QA), relevant to multimodal model evaluation and user interaction.
papers.title: Following Delegation Traces to Study Human Oversight in Interaction with Multimodal AI
papers.tldr: An online study shows that trust predicts how people delegate to multimodal AI, while observed delegation behavior captures experience-related factors that trust ratings miss.

papers.abstract: Recent post-training approaches have shown that self-supervised speech encoders can be adapted to learn a single utterance-level speech attribute through knowledge distillation. In this work, we investigate whether a single speech encoder can simultaneously preserve multiple complementary utterance-level speech representations. We propose a multi-attribute multi-teacher distillation framework that learns semantic, speaker, language, and emotion representations from four frozen teacher models using a shared SSL backbone and attribute-specific branches. Experiments on multilingual semantic retrieval, speaker verification, language identification, and speech emotion recognition show that the proposed model achieves performance close to dedicated single-task students while requiring only a single shared encoder. Furthermore, the learned layer aggregation strategies reveal that different speech attributes naturally emerge at different depths of the SSL encoder, providing new insights into the organization of speech representations.
authors: Maryem Bouziane, Salima Mdhaffar, Yannick Est\`eve
bullets: Addresses whether one self-supervised speech encoder can preserve multiple complementary utterance-level attributes.
Uses four frozen teacher models, a shared SSL backbone, and attribute-specific branches.
Evaluated on multilingual semantic retrieval, speaker verification, language identification, and emotion recognition.
Performance is close to dedicated single-task student models while using one shared encoder.
Layer aggregation results suggest different attributes emerge at different SSL encoder depths.
papers.selection_reason: Learns multiple speech attribute representations in a shared SSL encoder via multi-teacher distillation, relevant to multimodal representation learning.
papers.title: Learning Speech Attribute Representations via Multi-Teacher Distillation
papers.tldr: A multi-teacher distillation framework enables one speech encoder to retain semantic, speaker, language, and emotion representations with near-single-task performance.

papers.abstract: An agent that learns a user's preferences from their choices faces a cold start problem: before any choices are observed, it must rely solely on a prior. Informative priors are usually fitted to historical choice data, which new tasks and deployments lack. To address this, we present Agentic-Priors, which lets agentic systems use the implicit knowledge of large language models (LLMs) instead. Specifically, an LLM states a new user's trade-offs in interpretable terms, such as willingness to pay or value of time, which we map to a prior over multinomial logit coefficients. This prior is then refined by a Bayesian learner as choices are observed. Across seven choice datasets, Agentic-Priors improves cold start accuracy over an uninformed prior by 5-40 percentage points. It also outperforms AutoElicit, a state-of-the-art LLM prior-elicitation method, on three datasets and loses on one. It is up to 18 points more accurate than in-context learning, and never significantly worse. Against hierarchical Bayes models fitted to surveys of increasing size, our approach is worth roughly 6-40 surveyed users, in terms of log-loss, so its value is concentrated in a deployment's first users.
authors: Bruno Arcanjo, Zhaoxing Li, Sebastian Stein
bullets: Addresses preference elicitation when no user choices are yet available.
An LLM describes a new user’s trade-offs, which are mapped to priors over multinomial logit coefficients.
A Bayesian learner updates these priors as user choices accumulate.
Across seven choice datasets, it improves cold-start accuracy over an uninformed prior by 5–40 percentage points.
Its benefit is concentrated among early users, with performance comparable to information from roughly 6–40 surveyed users in log-loss terms.
papers.selection_reason: Uses LLMs to generate informative priors for test-time preference elicitation, addressing the cold start problem in adaptive systems.
papers.title: Agentic-Priors: Using Large Language Models to Address the Cold Start Problem in Preference Elicitation
papers.tldr: Agentic-Priors uses LLM-derived, interpretable preference trade-offs to provide informative priors that substantially improve cold-start preference learning.

papers.abstract: Vision--language pre-training has enabled substantial progress in image--text retrieval and zero-shot recognition by learning transferable cross-modal representations. However, sentence-level alignment remains insufficient for compositional matching, where captions can describe the same objects and attributes while differing in how these elements are bound. To address this limitation, we propose Flow-CLIP, which refines global image-text alignment through image-conditioned changes in token--patch evidence. Global Compatibility Calibration (GCC) learns a sentence-level similarity metric, while Image-Conditioned Evidence Refinement (ICER) incorporates visual patch context into token queries and uses the resulting change in local matching evidence to adjust the global score. We further introduce Cross-Image Margin Ranking (CIMR), which compares the same positive--negative caption pair across matched and mismatched images, encouraging a larger ranking margin when the image supports the correct description. Experiments on compositional matching and attribute--object binding benchmarks show that Flow-CLIP improves binding accuracy over pretrained CLIP and learned global alignment through local evidence refinement, while cross-image ranking supervision mitigates reliance on language priors. Code will be released at link.
authors: Minghong Wei, Enguang Zhu, Pu Cao, Lu Yang, Qing Song
bullets: Targets sentence-level alignment failures where captions mention the same elements but bind attributes and objects differently.
Combines Global Compatibility Calibration (GCC) with Image-Conditioned Evidence Refinement (ICER) to adjust global scores using changes in local visual evidence.
Uses Cross-Image Margin Ranking (CIMR) to reduce reliance on language priors by comparing caption pairs across matched and mismatched images.
Improves binding accuracy over pretrained CLIP and learned global alignment on compositional matching and attribute–object binding benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Improves compositional image-text matching, a multimodal foundation model technique.
papers.title: Flow-CLIP: Image-Conditioned Residual Scoring for CompositionalImage-Text Matching
papers.tldr: Flow-CLIP improves compositional image–text matching by refining global similarity with image-conditioned token–patch evidence and cross-image ranking.

papers.abstract: Many vision-language-action policies rely on action-labeled robot demonstrations and lack an explicit mechanism for predicting future visual states. These limitations hinder learning from action-free videos and can encourage overfitting to demonstration conditions, weakening generalization and robustness. We present TS-WAM, a lightweight Teacher-Student World-Action Model that addresses these challenges through self-supervised temporal learning and explicit future prediction. Its vlm-jepa framework learns from heterogeneous data, including robot demonstrations and action-free human videos, using an EMA target branch without requiring a separately trained external teacher. By coupling vlm-jepa with delta-lwm, TS-WAM learns to predict latent actions from the current observation and instruction and uses them to predict future visual features that guide action generation at inference. A unified end-to-end training architecture jointly optimizes temporal representation learning, visual dynamics, and robot control without a separate latent-action or world-model pretraining stage. The EMA target branch is removed at inference, keeping the deployed policy lightweight. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv, together with real-world manipulation experiments on Franka Research 3 and RevoTron, demonstrate that TS-WAM achieves strong manipulation performance, generalization, and robustness.
authors: Menghao Yin, Jiaju Yin, Xiyue Dong, Lixin Xu, Zhenhui Zhang, Ke Zhang, Yating Feng, Renjing Xu
bullets: Addresses reliance on action-labeled demonstrations and limited future-state modeling in vision-language-action policies.
Uses self-supervised temporal learning with an EMA target branch to train on heterogeneous robot and human-video data without an external teacher.
Couples latent-action prediction with future visual-feature prediction to guide action generation at inference.
Jointly trains temporal representations, visual dynamics, and robot control end to end, without separate latent-action or world-model pretraining.
Shows strong manipulation performance, generalization, and robustness in simulated benchmarks and real-world experiments.
papers.selection_reason: Jointly learns temporal latent actions, future visual prediction, and robot control from demonstrations and human videos.
papers.title: TS-WAM: Temporal Latent Actions and World-Action Coupling for Vision-Language Robot Control
papers.tldr: TS-WAM is a lightweight vision-language-action policy that learns from both robot demonstrations and action-free videos by predicting latent actions and future visual states for more robust control.

papers.abstract: Language-guided 3D affordance grounding aims to localize functional regions on 3D objects according to interaction intents. However, existing methods exhibit poor generalization to unseen objects. One challenge is the query-target gap: a semantic discrepancy between query features encoding interaction intents and target-region features, leading to inaccurate grounding. End-to-end training favors query representations tailored to seen objects, limiting their compatibility with shifted target-region features on unseen objects. To address this issue, we propose BridgeAfford, a framework that reduces the query-target semantic gap from two complementary perspectives. First, Interaction Region Alignment (IRA) promotes cross-object alignment among geometrically similar interaction regions during training. This enables structures on unseen objects that resemble previously observed ones to produce representations similar to those learned during training, facilitating target-region recognition. Second, Visual Evidence Aggregation (VEA) leverages a 2D affordance model to refine the attention distribution and guide the query toward the correct region, yielding more target-aware queries. Extensive experiments on the LASO and PIAD datasets demonstrate that BridgeAfford outperforms existing methods, particularly on unseen objects, highlighting its robust generalization ability.
authors: Yijie Su, Yakun Zhu, Yi Bin, Pengpeng Zeng, Liang Chen, Guoqing Wang, Jingkuan Song, Heng Tao Shen
bullets: Targets poor generalization caused by mismatched query and target-region representations.
Interaction Region Alignment aligns geometrically similar interaction regions across objects during training.
Visual Evidence Aggregation uses a 2D affordance model to refine attention and make queries more target-aware.
Experiments on LASO and PIAD show improved performance, especially for unseen objects.
Scope: focuses on generalization to shifted or previously unseen 3D objects.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes BridgeAfford for generalizable 3D affordance grounding, addressing the query-target gap and generalization in 3D foundation models.
papers.title: BridgeAfford: Bridging Query-Target Gap for Generalizable 3D Affordance Grounding
papers.tldr: BridgeAfford improves language-guided 3D affordance grounding on unseen objects by narrowing the semantic gap between interaction queries and target regions.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are typically trained with action prediction as the primary supervision signal, since robots ultimately execute actions. Auxiliary objectives such as latent-action (LA) and future-vision (FV) prediction are often added to improve policy learning, yet they compete with action prediction for the same training budget. We ask whether, under a fixed budget, allocating a substantial share of training samples to such objectives, rather than to further action prediction, can improve policy learning. We build a unified VLA framework that couples a two-stream multimodal diffusion transformer (MMDiT) with a sample-level router, which assigns each training sample to either action prediction or an auxiliary objective and thus makes supervision allocation explicit. Within this framework, we instantiate three LA targets based on LAPA and its DINO-feature variants, and three FV targets based on DINOv3, V-JEPA 2, and Wan2.2 representations. Across LIBERO, CALVIN, and four real-robot tasks, suitable LA and FV supervision outperforms action-only training under the same budget, even when action prediction receives no more than half of the training samples. FV generally outperforms LA, although the strongest LA target remains competitive on CALVIN.
