Evaluated on structured verbal and linguistic interactions, our architecture successfully detects MCI with a classification accuracy of 0.733 +- 0.13 and an F1-score of 0.716 +- 0.14, outperforming advanced baselines. The framework provides a mathematically rigorous, scalable, and robust foundation for home-based, real-time dementia screening.
authors: Sankalp Vaish, Sumukh Veeramalla, Rishank Singh, Caroline Summerour, John A. Batsis, Xiaohui Liang
bullets: Introduces a behavioral dataset spanning seven unscripted multimodal interactions over 18 months.
Represents continuous sessions as a dense Batch × Session × Time × Feature 4D tensor.
Uses hierarchical modeling: intra-session regression slopes capture acute behavioral fading, while inter-session cross-attention accumulates longitudinal drift.
A localized Quality Gate filters low-integrity features and fuses semantic information with physical behavioral dynamics.
On structured verbal and linguistic interactions, achieves 0.733 ± 0.13 accuracy and 0.716 ± 0.14 F1; scope is limited to the reported interaction setting.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical 4D Transformer for multimodal temporal behavioral modeling; transferable to video understanding.
papers.title: CogDrift-4D: Hierarchical Multimodal Modeling of Temporal Behavioral Decay for MCI Detection
papers.tldr: CogDrift-4D models short- and long-term behavioral decline across multimodal interactions to support scalable MCI detection.

papers.abstract: Vehicles that lose control at the handling limit through icing, hydroplaning, or an abrupt evasive maneuver fall outside the operating envelope of production safety systems such as electronic stability control, which focus on preventing instability rather than recovering from it. Expert drivers regain authority in these conditions by drifting. Existing autonomous recovery approaches are validated on idealized scenarios, define "recovered" states empirically and inconsistently, or rely on offline-planned trajectories rather than acting online. We address these gaps by first training a racing policy with reinforcement learning that learns drifting as a time-optimal maneuver, then adapting it to recovery through continued training with a minimum-time reward. We define recovery relative to a phase-plane-grounded stable equilibrium and introduce Gym-Khana for controller training and evaluation. Across 294 initial loss-of-control states, the transferred policy improves recovery by 186.8% over a Stanley path tracker and outperforms both a nonlinear model predictive controller and a recovery-only policy trained from scratch, while also recovering faster on states the baseline can already handle. An ablation shows that racing pretraining, rather than broader initial-state exposure alone, drives this gain. Deployed on a physical 1:10-scale F1TENTH vehicle using system identification, actuator-lag modelling, and domain randomization, the transferred policy outperforms Stanley on every tested loss-of-control state, including recovering 50% of the time from a hard state the baseline never recovers from.
authors: Teodor Ilie, Kleber Cabral, Sidney Givigi
bullets: Targets failures beyond production electronic stability control, including icing, hydroplaning, and abrupt evasive maneuvers.
Pretrains a policy to drift as a time-optimal racing maneuver, then adapts it for recovery with continued minimum-time training.
Defines recovery using a phase-plane-grounded stable equilibrium and introduces Gym-Khana for training and evaluation.
Across 294 simulated initial states, the transferred policy improves recovery by 186.8% over a Stanley path tracker and outperforms nonlinear MPC and recovery-only training.
On a 1:10-scale F1TENTH vehicle, it outperforms Stanley on every tested state and recovers 50% of the time from a state the baseline never recovers from.
papers.selection_reason: RL racing pretraining transferred to autonomous loss-of-control recovery, relevant to learned robot control.
papers.title: Race to Recovery: Designing Advanced Safety Systems for Autonomous Driving via Learning Autonomous Racing
papers.tldr: A racing-trained reinforcement-learning policy can recover autonomous vehicles from severe loss-of-control states more effectively than conventional and recovery-specific controllers.

papers.abstract: Realistic traffic simulation and autonomous planning both depend on modeling interactions among heterogeneous road users whose dynamics, constraints, and behaviors differ fundamentally. Existing approaches predominantly learn realistic interaction behavior from large-scale human driving demonstrations. In this work, we ask whether such behavior can instead emerge purely through self-play. We present SHRED, a framework that jointly trains vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists through large-scale heterogeneous self-play from random initialization, without demonstrations or logged-trajectory replay. SHRED combines type-specific dynamics and objectives with procedural scenario generation and per-agent randomization, allowing diverse behaviors to emerge through closed-loop interaction. On the Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge (WOSAC), SHRED jointly controls all three road-user types and outperforms both the closest demonstration-free self-play baseline and prior self-play methods that use demonstration-trained reference policies. Policies trained only on nuPlan map geometry retain comparable realism under zero-shot evaluation on Waymo. For planning, SHRED outperforms all compared planners on the interaction-heavy InterPlan benchmark. Controlled ablations show that heterogeneity in self-play improves both traffic realism and planning performance, with particularly large planning gains in interaction-heavy scenarios. Together, these results establish heterogeneous procedural self-play as a scalable, demonstration-free paradigm for learning realistic and interactive traffic behavior.
authors: Wei-Jer Chang, Zhouchonghao Wu, Akshay Rangesh, Weixin Li, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Wei Zhan
bullets: Addresses the need for realistic multi-agent traffic behavior without relying on human driving demonstrations or logged trajectories.
Jointly trains heterogeneous road users from random initialization using type-specific dynamics and objectives, procedural scenarios, and per-agent randomization.
Outperforms demonstration-free and prior demonstration-assisted self-play baselines on WOSAC while controlling all three road-user types.
Policies trained on nuPlan map geometry maintain comparable realism in zero-shot Waymo evaluation and outperform compared planners on the interaction-heavy InterPlan benchmark.
Ablations show that heterogeneous self-play improves both realism and planning, especially in interaction-heavy scenarios.
papers.selection_reason: Learns interactive driving and traffic behavior through self-play for autonomous planning, matching learned navigation/planning interests.
papers.title: SHRED: Self-Play for Heterogeneous Road-Users without Expert Demonstrations
papers.tldr: SHRED learns realistic, interactive behavior for vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists through heterogeneous self-play alone, without expert demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding pairs a cheap drafter with parallel verification against the target. At ultra-long context it stops paying, because a drafter that attends over the full prefix inherits the target's context-dependent cost, so the speedup it was meant to provide first erodes and then reverses. The standard response is to build a long-context drafter, by training or fine-tuning one, or by using a multi-token-prediction head shipped inside the target checkpoint. We argue this is unnecessary, because the drafters in use are target-conditioned, reading hidden states the target computed over the entire prefix, so distant context already reaches them without their own attention, and verification corrects what they miss. We therefore freeze released short-context drafters and run them far past their training length under two inference-time mechanisms, one bounding the attention cache they see, which fixes their cost, and one re-basing their rotary position indices into the trained range. No weight is touched and the only tunable saturates early, so one vLLM-side configuration spans 4k to two million tokens, costing at most 0.16x of speedup at short length. We prove when a common index shift leaves the drafter's computation exactly unchanged, and decompose acceptance into two measurable gaps with sharp bounds. Whatever speedup a frozen drafter delivers at short context, it retains out to two million tokens, across three target-drafter pairs and five corpora. The claim concerns the flatness rather than the multiple, and removing either mechanism eliminates it. The gain is conditional on the speculative cost per emitted token staying below the matched target-only cost.
authors: Aref Jafari, Vansh Bhatia, Matt Qin, Subhajit Dutta Chowdhury, Ben Lee, Vikram Appia, Ali Ghodsi, Mehdi Rezagholizadeh
bullets: Long-context drafting becomes uneconomical when the drafter attends over the full prefix.
The approach freezes existing drafters and uses bounded attention-cache visibility plus rotary-position re-basing, with no weight updates.
A single vLLM-side configuration covers 4k–2M-token contexts; tuning saturates early and costs at most 0.16× short-context speedup.
Across three target–drafter pairs and five corpora, the drafter retains its short-context speedup up to two million tokens.
The result concerns stable speedup rather than its absolute magnitude and depends on speculative decoding remaining cheaper per emitted token than target-only decoding.
papers.selection_reason: Long-context speculative decoding with frozen short-context drafters.
papers.title: Long-Context Drafting Does Not Require Long-Context Drafters
papers.tldr: Frozen short-context drafters can support speculative decoding at up to two-million-token contexts when inference-time cache and position handling prevent their cost from growing with context length.

papers.abstract: Negation is a fundamental aspect of language understanding and it is important vision-language models (VLMs) are able to process it effectively. We investigate how VLMs process negation by analysing attention patterns of different models. We draw comparisons between human gaze and attention in models when processing affirmative vs negated statements. We compare object level model attention to human eye-fixations in both binary and multary settings, evaluating with both synthetic and realistic datasets. We find models generally do not follow human-like attention patterns when resolving negation, suggesting they rely on mechanisms outside of attention. While layerwise analysis shows that PaliGemma2-3B shifts object attention to the alternative under negation, our headwise ablations suggest this is a byproduct rather than a negation processing mechanism. Additionally, we find that LLaVA-1.5-7B displays a spatial bias towards left-side objects. Our evaluation of models on downstream tasks shows that all models have a discrepancy between affirmative and negated questions highlighting the need to better understand the underlying processing of negation to close this performance gap. Code available at https://github.com/otmive/negation_attention
authors: Beth Pearson, Michael Wray, Martha Lewis
bullets: The study compares model object attention with human eye fixations across affirmative and negated statements.
It evaluates binary and multary settings using both synthetic and realistic datasets.
PaliGemma2-3B shifts attention toward the alternative object under negation, but ablations suggest this is not the underlying negation mechanism.
LLaVA-1.5-7B shows a spatial bias toward objects on the left.
All evaluated models perform differently on affirmative versus negated downstream questions, highlighting a persistent negation-processing gap.
papers.selection_reason: Directly studies attention and reasoning in vision-language models, fitting multimodal LLM analysis.
papers.title: Probing Negation Understanding in Vision-Language Models With Object Attention
papers.tldr: Vision-language models’ object-attention patterns generally do not resemble human gaze when processing negation, revealing unresolved differences in how they handle affirmative versus negated statements.

papers.abstract: Skill-policy co-evolution, in which an agent's policy model and its skill bank improve each other during training, is a promising paradigm for self-improving agents. Current evaluations score the co-evolved policy on the final bank it trained with (the delivered bank). After deployment, however, skills may be rewritten, added or removed more frequently than the policy model is retrained, leaving the policy to operate on a drifted skill bank that neither the training objective nor existing evaluation protocols address. In this paper, we first establish, through theoretical and empirical analysis, that the fragility hidden by this blind spot is not incidental. The acceptance rule these methods share (cooperative acceptance) ties a policy's competence to the bank it co-evolved with, leaving it fragile once skills drift, regardless of the implementation; empirically, sensitivity to skill drift grows as co-evolution training proceeds. We therefore introduce the CO-evolution Drift Audit (CODA), a deployment-oriented evaluation protocol that simulates skill drift and, alongside success rate under worst-case drift, introduces two new metrics: a consistency rate under meaning-preserving edits and a resistance rate to corrupted skills. Across four co-evolution methods and five benchmarks (six settings), worst-case success is 5-13 points below the peak measured for each delivered pair, erasing 52-93% of the delivered bank's gain over the no-skill baseline. CODA thus reframes the target of co-evolution, from peak performance on the co-evolved bank to the ability to harness skills however they evolve, and provides a shared standard against which future methods can be audited.
authors: Yujie Feng, Xiaobin Wang, Jinluan Yang, Xiaonan Shi, Pengjun Xie, Philip S. Yu, Xiaoming Wu, Jieping Ye
bullets: Existing evaluations test policies only on the skill bank used during co-evolution, overlooking post-deployment drift.
Theoretical and empirical analysis shows cooperative acceptance intrinsically couples policy competence to its co-evolved bank.
CODA simulates skill drift and measures worst-case success, consistency under meaning-preserving edits, and resistance to corrupted skills.
Across four methods and five benchmarks, drift reduced success by 5–13 points and erased 52–93% of gains over no-skill baselines.
The protocol shifts evaluation from peak performance on a fixed bank to robustness as skills evolve.
papers.selection_reason: Audits skill-policy co-evolution under skill drift, directly relevant to continual learning and self-improving agents.
papers.title: Evolving Together, Failing Apart: The Skill-Policy Co-evolution Trap in Self-Improving Agents
papers.tldr: Skill-policy co-evolution can produce agents that perform well only with their original skill bank, so CODA evaluates robustness to realistic skill drift.

papers.abstract: Map generation tasks feature extensive non-structural vectorized data (e.g., points, polylines, and polygons) and thus pose significant challenges to common pixel-wise generative models. Conventional approaches use multiple stages, first segmenting these features at the pixel level and then performing vectorized post-processing, with errors and complexity compounding at each stage. Motivated by the recent success of auto-regressive language modeling, we propose the first map foundation model, named Map Auto-Regressor (MARS), that is capable of generating both multi-polyline road networks and polygon buildings in a unified manner. For training MARS, we collected to our knowledge the largest multi-class map extraction dataset totaling 3.4M examples, which we call MAP-3M. Across four road and building datasets, MARS outperforms or matches the performance of multistage baselines. Additionally, we develop a "Chat with MARS" capability that enables interactive human-in-the-loop map generation and correction, supported by the auto-regressive nature of our end-to-end approach. We release our MAP-3M dataset and project demo page at (1) https://huggingface.co/datasets/bag-lab/MAP-3M and (2) https://huggingface.co/spaces/bag-lab/MARS, respectively.
authors: Qi Zhang, Suvam Bag, Rupanjali Kukal, Lucas Thai, Jacob Kovarskiy, Mike Bianco, Xiaojie Guo, Raphael Tang, Mikael Figueroa, Rishi Madhok, Nikolaos Karianakis, Fuxun Yu
bullets: Addresses the complexity and error accumulation of conventional pixel-wise, multistage map-generation pipelines.
Unifies generation of multi-polyline roads and polygon buildings in an end-to-end autoregressive framework.
Trained on MAP-3M, a 3.4M-example multi-class map extraction dataset.
Across four road and building datasets, matches or surpasses multistage baselines.
Supports interactive human correction through a “Chat with MARS” capability; the dataset and demo are released publicly.
papers.selection_reason: Autoregressive map foundation model generating vectorized road networks and buildings; directly relevant to spatial layout understanding and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: MARS - A foundational map auto-regressor
papers.tldr: MARS is an autoregressive foundation model that directly generates vectorized road networks and building polygons, avoiding multistage pixel segmentation and post-processing.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric, but what shape does the world take inside the policy that performs it? Prior work on vision-language-action (VLA) policies establishes that task-relevant variables are linearly readable from activations, yet readability certifies only that a variable is present and says nothing about the shape its values trace, which may be curved and multi-dimensional. Using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we build a taxonomy of seven task-relevant concepts in VLA models. We find that realized geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and is shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts. Physical joint limits, for example, leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, and distance to the target, a single scalar, is realized in two orthogonal subspaces, a coarse ruler for the approach and a fine ruler for the grasp. The same geometries reappear in two further VLA models on real-world robot data, indicating that they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation. We demonstrate how the findings are actionable by steering along the geometry a concept realizes. Overall, this work lays out an initial phenomenology of realized geometry in VLA policies and demonstrates that a concept's shape carries as much importance as its readability.
authors: Mozes Jacobs, Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Siddharth Boppana, Fenil R. Doshi, Usha Bhalla, Thomas Icard, Matt Feiszli, Thomas McGrath, Vasudev Shyam, Demba Ba, Leon Bergen, Nina Miolane, Owen Lewis, Jack Merullo, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Atticus Geiger, Matthew Kowal, Thomas Fel
bullets: Maps seven task-relevant concepts using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions.
Finds geometries are predominantly multi-dimensional and reflect the constraints under which the robot acts.
Shows joint limits turn wrist orientation into an open arc, while target distance forms separate coarse- and fine-scale subspaces.
Observes similar geometries across two additional VLAs using real-world robot data, suggesting the patterns are not model- or simulation-specific.
Demonstrates that understanding a concept’s geometry enables targeted activation steering.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes representational geometry in vision-language-action policies for robotic manipulation, directly relevant to embodied VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: A Phenomenology of Neural Geometry in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: VLA policies encode task-relevant concepts as structured, often multi-dimensional geometries shaped by physical and task constraints—not merely as linearly readable variables.

papers.abstract: Damage-recovery algorithms often rank gaits from short trials, yet a gait that performs well briefly may not remain effective during continued execution. In reset-free recovery, each trial also changes the physical state inherited by the next. We introduce persistent profile-guided reset-free recovery (PGRR), which predicts multiple outcomes over repeated gait execution and uses conservative uncertainty-aware estimates to guide short online probes without resetting the robot. Across 108 matched MuJoCo tasks spanning leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock, PGRR improves final quality by 0.106 and slot-averaged recovery quality (SRQ) by 0.044 relative to an IT&E-inspired Gaussian-process baseline, while reducing low-quality failures by 27.8 percentage points. Final-quality gains occur in all three damage classes. Against no adaptation, PGRR also improves final quality and reduces low-quality failures, whereas the aggregate SRQ difference is inconclusive. Development ablations identify conservative uncertainty handling as the clearest supported contributor to the observed gains. These results show that PGRR can identify stronger post-damage gaits under continuous physical state and that final-gait quality and recovery-summary performance provide complementary evidence for evaluating reset-free recovery.
authors: Minjoong Kim
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between short-trial gait rankings and long-term gait effectiveness after irreversible leg damage.
Uses persistent outcome profiles and conservative uncertainty-aware estimates to guide short online probes without resetting the robot.
Evaluated across 108 MuJoCo tasks involving leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock.
Improved final gait quality and reduced low-quality failures versus an IT&E-inspired Gaussian-process baseline; gains appeared across all damage classes.
Ablations most strongly supported conservative uncertainty handling, while aggregate SRQ improvement versus no adaptation was inconclusive.
papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty-guided reset-free gait recovery after leg damage, combining robot learning with online adaptation.
papers.title: Persistent Profile-Guided Reset-Free Recovery Improves Final Gait Selection after Irreversible Leg Damage
papers.tldr: PGRR improves the selection of durable post-damage gaits during reset-free recovery by modeling how repeated execution changes the robot’s physical state.

papers.abstract: Evaluator-guided reasoning presents a local control problem at every step: trust the current answer, return a fallback, or spend more inference. We formulate this choice as a compute-aware three-action controller, scoring terminal actions by predicted answer success and expansion by a rollout-based continuation-success surrogate, with compute cost priced explicitly. A local action-gap analysis characterizes when score errors can change a decision, while an expected regret bound accounts for errors along the realized expansion path. Guided by this analysis, we learn and calibrate action-specific confidence estimates, with local uncertainty penalties for ambiguous decisions. On held-out width expansion and revision tasks, the controller improves observed utility over calibration-selected fixed policies while reducing normalized online compute by about 30% and 16%, respectively. Across four Qwen3-8B seeds, compute is lower than fitted Q in both settings, while utility differences are small and mixed. The results frame evaluator-guided reasoning as resource allocation under uncertainty, rather than a uniformly stronger reasoner.
authors: Weida Liang, Kenji Kawaguchi
bullets: Formulates inference control as a compute-aware three-action decision problem.
Scores terminal actions by predicted success and expansion by rollout-based continuation success, with explicit compute costs.
Uses action-gap analysis, pathwise regret bounds, calibrated action confidence, and uncertainty penalties to guide decisions.
Improves observed utility over calibration-selected fixed policies while reducing normalized online compute by about 30% and 16% on two task types.
Results across four Qwen3-8B seeds show lower compute than fitted Q, but only small and mixed utility differences.
papers.selection_reason: Confidence-calibrated compute allocation for evaluator-guided test-time reasoning in LLMs.
papers.title: Confidence-Calibrated Inference Expansion for Evaluator-Guided Test-Time Reasoning
papers.tldr: A confidence-calibrated controller allocates test-time compute among answering, fallback, and further reasoning, improving utility while reducing online computation on evaluator-guided tasks.

papers.abstract: Despite their extensive pretraining knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, large language models (LLMs) struggle to adaptively gather information in experimental design tasks. We study how to amortize sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) into an LLM by explicitly training the reasoning that guides action selection using information-gain rewards. Our approach specifies the experimental generative model independently of the LLM's own beliefs, allowing us to optimize expected information gain under a model of our choosing. We investigate the design choices for amortization, including alternative generative-model constructions, reward estimation, hypothesis-space specification, multi-step objectives, and computational costs relative to training- and inference-time BED baselines. On Twenty Questions, the resulting policies improve information acquisition and task performance, outperform inference- and training-time BED baselines at substantially lower computational cost, and generalize to unseen categories. We further demonstrate positive transfer from Twenty Questions training to Medi-Q, a real-world clinical dialogue benchmark. These results suggest that information gathering can be learned as a generalizable reasoning skill in LLMs.
authors: Anita Kriz, Antonin Berthon, Nicol\'as Astorga, Mihaela van der Schaar
bullets: LLMs often struggle to adaptively select informative actions despite strong reasoning and pretrained knowledge.
The method amortizes sequential Bayesian experimental design by training reasoning with information-gain rewards under an independently specified generative model.
The study evaluates generative-model design, reward estimation, hypothesis spaces, multi-step objectives, and computational costs.
On Twenty Questions, the learned policies improve information acquisition and task performance, generalize to unseen categories, and use less computation than BED baselines.
Training on Twenty Questions transfers positively to the real-world Medi-Q clinical dialogue benchmark.
papers.selection_reason: Trains LLMs to amortize sequential experimental design as a generalizable reasoning skill.
papers.title: Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs
papers.tldr: The paper trains LLMs to learn efficient, generalizable information-gathering strategies for sequential experimental design.

papers.abstract: Reasoning distillation requires chain-of-thought (CoT) data with correct answers, but obtaining such data efficiently remains challenging. Forward CoT generation (FCG) followed by rejection sampling (RS) produces verified, question-only responses, yet may require many teacher calls for difficult problems. Reverse CoT generation (RCG) is cheaper because it conditions on the known answer, but access to this answer can lead to post-hoc rationalization and a mismatch with the student's answer-free inference setting. We propose CoTranslator, which learns to translate reverse CoT responses toward the distribution of verified forward responses. Trained on a small set of paired reverse and rejection-sampled forward responses, it supports large-scale generation and verification of student training data. Across six student models evaluated on six mathematics benchmarks, CoTranslator improves average accuracy over semantic suppression by up to $5.82$ percentage points. For two 4B students, it retains $95.0\%$ of rejection sampling's average accuracy while using $35.9\%$ of its estimated compute. Without retraining, the same translator transfers to a new mathematics dataset, a different teacher, and STEM problems, improving average STEM accuracy by $4.88$ and $4.31$ percentage points for 4B and 8B students, respectively. These results show that CoTranslator offers an efficient and transferable approach to reasoning distillation.
authors: Zinan Tang, Zhuoshi Pan, Kairui Chen, Ze Yan, Shaomian Zheng, Yukun Zhang, Gang Wang, Biqing Huang
bullets: Problem: Forward CoT generation with rejection sampling is costly, while reverse CoT can rationalize from known answers and mismatch student inference.
Method: Train a translator on a small set of paired reverse and verified forward responses, then use it to generate and verify large-scale distillation data.
Results: Across six student models and six math benchmarks, it improves accuracy over semantic suppression by up to 5.82 percentage points.
Efficiency: For 4B students, it retains 95.0% of rejection sampling’s average accuracy using 35.9% of its estimated compute.
Transferability: Without retraining, it improves STEM accuracy by 4.88 points for 4B students and 4.31 points for 8B students on new settings.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient reasoning distillation method for LLMs via reverse-to-forward CoT translation.
papers.title: CoTranslator: Reverse to Forward Chain-of-Thought Translator for Reasoning Distillation
papers.tldr: CoTranslator makes cheaper answer-conditioned reasoning data more suitable for answer-free student training by translating it toward verified forward chain-of-thought responses.

papers.abstract: We investigate whether per-layer, per-task-phase (prompt/reasoning/response) expert-routing statistics in a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model can guide layer-wise mixed-precision quantization of routed-expert FFN tensors (down/gate and up). To attain layerwise routing statistics, we build a routing-capture and profiling pipeline for Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B in ik_llama.cpp, derive a composite sensitivity score from routing entropy/decisiveness, coefficient of variation (CV), Jaccard/phase-fragility, and top-1 expert strength, and use coordinate descent to tune a layer allocation that respects a fixed average bits-per-weight budget. Notably, the profiling pipeline is applicable to standard top-k MoE architectures. Across independent experimental conditions (about 4.0 bpw flat, about 2.7 bpw steep, and about 2.7 bpw random allocation as a control), reallocation fails to outperform the uniform baseline within each quality tier. In the flat regime, reallocation is statistically neutral (z about 0.9). For the steep tier, the random reallocation performs within 1 SE of the routing-guided reallocation at the same tier, indicating a structural loss at this quality rung caused by mandatory downgrades and Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KLD) tail injection. This aggressive-budget condition shows a decisive loss (z greater than 4 SE) replicated across three independent weight vectors. We argue that the deeper issue is that routing-behavior statistics are an unvalidated proxy for true per-layer quantization cost.
authors: Yifan Liu
bullets: The study tests whether routing entropy, decisiveness, variability, phase fragility, and top-1 expert strength can guide layer-wise bit allocation.
A routing-capture pipeline profiles Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B in ik_llama.cpp and uses coordinate descent under fixed average bit budgets.
Routing-guided reallocation does not outperform uniform allocation in the tested quality tiers; at the flatter budget it is statistically neutral.
At the aggressive budget, mandatory downgrades and KLD-tail injection cause a replicated quality loss, while random reallocation performs similarly to routing-guided allocation.
The results suggest routing behavior is an unvalidated proxy for true per-layer quantization cost.
papers.selection_reason: Quantization sensitivity analysis for efficient MoE LLM inference.
papers.title: Task-Phase-Conditioned Expert Routing Is Not a Reliable Proxy for Quantization Sensitivity in MoE FFN Tensors
papers.tldr: Routing statistics by task phase do not reliably identify which MoE expert FFN layers are most sensitive to mixed-precision quantization.

papers.abstract: Wolof is spoken by 23M people, mostly in Senegal, but remains weakly supported by open-weight language models, while API models raise cost, governance, and sovereignty constraints for local deployments. In this paper, we present 0.6B-14B open-weight models adapted to Wolof through instruction tuning, preference alignment, and model merging. After presenting the pipeline and data, extensive experiments on 63~public and in-house tasks show good performance on Wolof understanding and generation while remaining effective on other languages and cross-lingual skills, with the 8B and 14B models being particularly competitive with substantially larger commercial systems. The models are currently being evaluated in internal customer-care pilots and are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Orange/wolof-lm .
authors: Gw\'enol\'e Lecorv\'e, Delphine Charlet, Pierre Adam, Floriane Behanzin, Lionel Delphin-Poulat, Johannes Heinecke, G\'eraldine Damnati, Pelin Kaytmaz, Nourredine Khaous, Charbel Kindji, Meriam Maadi, Abdoulaye Mbaye, Claire Perroux, Isma\"el Rousseau, Papa S\'ega Wad\'e, Gilles Xiberras, Olivier Zhang, Malek Zitouni
bullets: Addresses limited open-weight support for Wolof and the cost, governance, and sovereignty concerns of API-based models.
Adapts models using instruction tuning, preference alignment, and model merging.
Evaluates the models across 63 public and in-house tasks covering Wolof understanding, generation, multilingual, and cross-lingual capabilities.
Reports strong Wolof performance while retaining effectiveness in other languages; the 8B and 14B models are competitive with substantially larger commercial systems.
Models are undergoing customer-care pilot evaluations and are publicly available on Hugging Face.
papers.selection_reason: Open-weight LLMs adapted to Wolof via instruction tuning and alignment.
papers.title: Wolof-Adapted Industry-Ready Open-Weight Language Models
papers.tldr: This paper introduces open-weight Wolof language models from 0.6B to 14B parameters designed for practical, locally deployable use.

papers.abstract: A mesh of interceptors defending a fixed site must spread over the predicted arrival point of an approaching object. This is a recurring task in multi-agent robotics: N agents, each covering a disc of radius r, spread over a probability density so that a point drawn from it falls within some agent's disc. We give closed forms for the quantities that bound performance before any policy is chosen, and validate each by Monte Carlo. The uncertainty of a point predicted by extrapolating a noisy linear track follows from least-squares variance propagation plus a delta-method term for the uncertain arrival time, agreeing with simulation to within 1.8%. The coverage probability of a packed mesh admits a closed form accurate to 0.007 absolute, with a volumetric analogue. A naive area ratio misses a ceiling: while agents stay at least 2r apart, no mesh exceeds 90.69% coverage in the plane or 74.05% in a volume. This ceiling belongs to the separation constraint, not to the problem - permitting overlap substitutes Kershner's thinnest-covering density and removes it, the better regime above a crossover at p=0.80. Hexagonal packing is optimal among five arrangements; the centroidal-Voronoi configuration coverage control supplies reaches only half its coverage at small budgets. The Gaussian assumption is conservative under heavy tails and anisotropy but fragile under bias: a one-sigma aim-point offset costs 14 points of coverage. A repositioning team must also choose a commit time, and the admissible window can be empty. Against the applicable ceiling, analytic placement attains 85% of what the configuration permits while centralised PPO averages 15% over three trainer seeds, with a paired bootstrap against a null policy containing zero at every seed. We argue such ceilings should be computed before any learning experiment and quoted alongside every result.
authors: Dmytro Babarytskyi
bullets: Closed-form bounds estimate arrival-point uncertainty, mesh coverage, packing limits, and the admissible repositioning commit window.
With non-overlapping agents, coverage is capped at 90.69% in 2D and 74.05% in 3D; overlap removes this separation-induced ceiling above a crossover of p=0.80.
Analytic placement reaches 85% of the applicable ceiling, whereas centralized PPO averages 15% across three training seeds.
Gaussian uncertainty is conservative under heavy tails and anisotropy but sensitive to bias: a one-standard-deviation aim-point offset reduces coverage by 14 percentage points.
The study validates its formulas by Monte Carlo and argues that feasibility ceilings should accompany learning results.
papers.selection_reason: Analytic feasibility bounds for multi-agent drone interception; relevant to embodied robot planning and informs learning-based navigation.
papers.title: Feasibility Ceilings Before Learning: Sizing and Timing Bounds for Drone-Mesh Interception
papers.tldr: Analytic feasibility ceilings reveal how well drone meshes can intercept uncertain arrivals before any policy is learned.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video models often generate the visual concepts requested in natural language prompts but fail to satisfy their intended ordering, timing, and persistence requirements. We propose representing these requirements as specifications in a formal Temporal Logic, and introduce Temporal Specification Guidance (TSG), a training-free inference-time framework that turns temporal specifications into executable objectives for guiding video generation during sampling. TSG scores traces of visual concept evidence using differentiable quantitative semantics and uses the score's gradients to construct a specification-guided denoising direction. We instantiate this framework with video-text attention traces, efficient differentiable scores for Metric Temporal Logic, and gradient-derived attention biases. This instantiation requires neither an external concept classifier nor backpropagation through the video transformer. Its attention-steered forward pass yields a denoising direction that augments classifier-free guidance (CFG). On a benchmark of 220 prompts spanning 11 categories of temporal constraints, including ordered object entry and state transitions, this instantiation improves specification satisfaction accuracy over CFG by 9.5-20 percentage points across five models, with minimal memory overhead. These results demonstrate the potential of temporal specifications and differentiable satisfaction objectives as a flexible interface for controlling video generation.
authors: Avishree Khare, Hideki Okamoto, Bardh Hoxha, Georgios Fainekos, Rajeev Alur
bullets: Targets failures in event ordering, timing, and persistence despite correct visual concepts.
Represents requirements in Metric Temporal Logic and scores visual concept attention traces with differentiable semantics.
Uses score gradients to create attention biases and a denoising direction that augments classifier-free guidance.
Evaluated on 220 prompts across 11 temporal-constraint categories and five models, improving satisfaction accuracy by 9.5–20 percentage points over CFG.
Requires no external concept classifier or backpropagation through the video transformer, with minimal memory overhead.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free temporal specification guidance for text-to-video diffusion models.
papers.title: Temporal Specification Guidance for Text-to-Video Generation
papers.tldr: Temporal Specification Guidance steers text-to-video sampling with formal temporal constraints, improving the correct timing and ordering of generated events without extra training or external classifiers.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal generation covers discrete, continuous, and hybrid paradigms. Discrete approaches with single-codebook visual tokenizers align naturally with text modeling but have limited representational capacity. Continuous and hybrid approaches retain richer visual representations, but they model text and images in heterogeneous spaces with different training objectives, potentially introducing optimization conflicts between modalities with misaligned representation spaces. These choices expose a central question: how to efficiently model high-capacity visual representations alongside textual content in a shared optimization space within a single backbone. We present Intern Lumina U2, to our knowledge the first diffusion language model to represent multi-codebook visual tokens in a fully discrete space. Each visual position is represented by a group of codes from complementary codebooks, increasing its representational capacity while preserving compatibility with discrete text modeling. At the input, the embeddings are concatenated at each position; at the output, a lightweight multi-codebook autoregressive head predicts the codes within each position sequentially, while the diffusion backbone processes all positions in parallel. Built on the unified 4D representation of AToken, Intern Lumina U2 supports image, video, and 3D inputs within a single backbone and achieves leading performance among unified models in visual understanding, image generation, and image editing. We further build a full-stack training, inference, and evaluation system on both Ascend and NVIDIA platforms to verify the cross-platform effectiveness of our model. We also improve the inference efficiency through a stability-aware sampling strategy, which combines confidence-plateau-guided unmasking approach with drift-triggered cache refreshing mechanisms, accelerating image generation by 4.45x.
authors: Qian Yu, Zongyang Qiu, Juncheng Yan, Hongliang Li, Qi Qin, Keqi Wang, Siqi Luo, Junkui Ju, Yapeng Mi, Tiantian Lu, Tian Liu, Pengyu Xie, Chenhao Ji, Minghui Zhang, Yiang Zhao, Siyu Yan, Haiying Xu, Yanbo Wang, Jianghan Shen, Yuandong Pu, Jiayi Lei, Borui Zhang, Jinxin Shi, Bo Zhang, Yuhang Zang, Shenglong Ye, Lixin Gu, Hongjie Zhang, Linghan Liu, Xinyuan Chen, Yuewen Cao, Lihe Zhang, Xiaohong Liu, Junjun He, Qiangwei Liu, Qi Zhang, Yu Cheng, Tianfan Xue, Hui Xiong, Chang Xu, Yu Qiao, Yihao Liu, Bin Fu
bullets: Addresses the limited capacity of single-codebook visual tokenizers and the optimization mismatch of hybrid continuous–discrete multimodal models.
Represents each visual position with complementary code groups, concatenating their embeddings and predicting codes sequentially with a lightweight head while denoising positions in parallel.
Built on AToken’s unified 4D representation to support image, video, and 3D inputs.
Reports leading performance among unified models for visual understanding, image generation, and image editing.
A stability-aware sampling strategy reportedly accelerates image generation by 4.45×, with cross-platform validation on Ascend and NVIDIA systems.
papers.selection_reason: Diffusion language model with multi-codebook discrete visual tokens for unified visual understanding and generation; relevant to multimodal foundation models and diffusion-based visual generation.
papers.title: Intern Lumina U2: A Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation
papers.tldr: Intern Lumina U2 is a diffusion language model that uses multiple discrete visual codebooks to unify text, image, video, and 3D understanding and generation in one backbone.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often trains language models on responses generated by a different, possibly stale behavior policy. Correcting this mismatch with learner-to-behavior importance weights can introduce high variance for long responses. We introduce Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization (GGPO), which minimizes a log-mean-exp contrast of KL-adjusted rewards among responses to the same prompt, without learner-to-behavior importance weights. We derive GGPO from KL-regularized policy optimization: on policy, its population loss is exactly the KL-regularized optimality gap, and under suitable coverage the learner's single-response expected reward is at least the behavior policy's best-of-$K$ reward, minus terms for the raw finite-group loss, regularization, and finite training data. We characterize reference refresh through exact Gibbs-target composition and a finite-data final-policy reward bound under local reference control and tokenwise behavior mismatch. This refresh is empirically important: in an ablation, fixed-reference GGPO scores $32.96$ on the five-benchmark problem-weighted average, versus $46.58$ with the default refresh schedule. Experiments on mathematical reasoning further show that GGPO outperforms GRPO and AGRO under training-inference mismatch and on fixed offline data, while maintaining its performance as controlled policy staleness grows.
authors: Xuanchang Zhang, Tong Zhang
bullets: Addresses learner–behavior policy mismatch, especially the high variance of importance weighting for long responses.
Uses a log-mean-exp contrast of KL-adjusted rewards among responses to the same prompt.
On-policy, the population loss equals the KL-regularized optimality gap; theory gives reward guarantees under coverage and reference-control conditions.
Reference refreshing is important: the reported five-benchmark average rises from 32.96 with a fixed reference to 46.58 with the default schedule.
On mathematical reasoning, GGPO outperforms GRPO and AGRO under training–inference mismatch and fixed offline data, and remains effective with increasing policy staleness.
papers.selection_reason: Off-policy RL method for verifiable-reward LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards
papers.tldr: GGPO optimizes verifiable-reward language models off-policy without high-variance importance weights, using KL-adjusted within-prompt reward contrasts and refreshed references.

papers.abstract: Generative gameplay requires more than immediate responses to player actions.Actions should have persistent consequences, while the generated world should act according to its own state and rules, shaping the player's situation and subsequent choices. Video generation captures local dynamics, but limited history, partially observed game state, and the need for contextual behavior decisions make such interactions difficult to sustain through audiovisual prediction alone. We introduce \rig (Reciprocally Interactive Generation), a framework for reciprocal interaction in generative gameplay. \rig combines persistent state and configurable rules, contextual interaction reasoning, and action-conditioned audiovisual generation. Together, these components make interaction consequences and actor behavior jointly determine generated content while maintaining consistency between game state and visible outcomes. We construct a Xonotic gameplay dataset to train an audiovisual generator for learning dynamics and interactions. Further post-training enables \rigarena, an interactive generative first-person shooter (FPS) prototype. Experiments demonstrate more reliable combat outcomes and reciprocal interaction between the player and the generated world. Project page: https://murphylmf.github.io/RIGen/.
authors: Mengfei Li, Yi Zhang, Xingtong Ge, Lunjie Zhu, Fangyu Lin, Peng Li, Guanglu Song, Yu Liu, Wei Xue, Wenhan Luo, Yike Guo
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of sustaining reciprocal, context-aware interactions through audiovisual prediction alone.
Combines persistent state and configurable rules with contextual reasoning and action-conditioned audiovisual generation.
Uses a Xonotic gameplay dataset to train an audiovisual generator for learning game dynamics and interactions.
Introduces RIGArena, an interactive generative FPS prototype created through further post-training.
Experiments report more reliable combat outcomes and stronger reciprocal interaction between the player and generated world.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned generative gameplay with persistent state and reciprocal interaction directly fits interactive world models and video world models.
papers.title: RIGen: Beyond Action Following with Reciprocal Interaction in Generative Gameplay
papers.tldr: RIGen enables generative gameplay where player actions have persistent consequences and the generated world responds according to its own state and rules.

papers.abstract: A self-improving agent has to decide which new skills to keep, and in practice it keeps whatever earns a high reward, convinces a judge model, or compresses its library, even when the skill is wrong. That is fine until the answers have to be exactly right: over a table of transactions, a total is either right or wrong. We ask a harder question: can an agent grow what it can compute with no reward, no judge, and no answer key, and still be exactly right? A single frozen model runs two nested loops over a small, exact domain-specific language (DSL). The inner loop answers new questions only when two independently written expressions agree on every record. The outer loop discovers its own missing capability and authors an operator for it, admitted only when an independent second implementation agrees and the result obeys a conservation law, all without ground truth. The inner loop roughly triples the answerable-question set, and the outer loop self-extends on disjoint starting sets, inventing operators outside the starting closure; a no-induction control answers none of the new questions. The admission rule is empirically sound: it rejects 138 of 138 buggy operator variants under an independent reference, even one written by a different model family, where the admit-if-it-runs, self-consistency, and compression signals the field relies on admit most of them. Unmodified, the same mechanism self-extends on two further domains with unrelated schemas, business-ledger and clinical-encounter question answering, growing their answerable sets more than tenfold and nearly twentyfold. The loop transfers across model families too: run with further proposers, the gate stays sound and independent families self-extend comparably, with only the induction yield tracking each proposer's DSL fluency.
authors: Yun-Shiuan Chuang, Yirou Ge, Yixi Li, Yiming Bian, Zijie Pan, Jenna L. Ballard, Uma Kona, Linsey Pang, Prakhar Mehrotra
bullets: Targets exact answers without rewards, judge models, or answer keys, where incorrect skills cannot be tolerated.
Uses nested loops: agreement between independent expressions answers questions, while agreement between independent operator implementations plus a conservation law admits new operators.
The inner loop roughly triples the answerable-question set; the outer loop discovers operators beyond the initial DSL closure and fails to expand without induction.
The admission rule rejects all 138 tested buggy operator variants under an independent reference, outperforming simpler admission signals in this evaluation.
The mechanism transfers to business-ledger and clinical-encounter domains, expanding answerable sets by more than tenfold and nearly twentyfold, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Self-improving agent that grows its own DSL through oracle-free operator induction; relevant to continual skill acquisition.
papers.title: A Self-Improving Agent that Grows its Own DSL: Oracle-Free Operator Induction for Exact Question Answering
papers.tldr: An oracle-free agent safely expands its exact-question-answering abilities by admitting only independently verified DSL operators that satisfy conservation laws.

papers.abstract: A reasoning trace retained at answer time plays two roles: it can raise accuracy, and it can compete with the current evidence when the two disagree. We disentangle these roles by crossing verified evidence versions with the traces generated from each and answering from the same traces and evidence under two configurations: continuation of the model's own thinking and a separate answer call. Across three model families (gpt-oss, Gemma4, Qwen3) on HotpotQA and MuSiQue, the separate call raises evidence-following over continuation by 29.9 to 60.6 points. On the same pairs, removing the trace lowers accuracy by similar amounts under both configurations. Yet continuation repeats the stale conclusion in most conflicts, and the separate call follows the current evidence far more often. Benefiting from a trace and deferring to it are therefore distinct properties. Further analyses show that the final line of a trace carries most of its value, gold evidence helps most before the trace is written, distractors weaken correction under a separate call, and renewed reasoning, unlike a verification instruction, follows the current evidence in most conflicts. Because trace deletion alone cannot reveal which source an answer follows, evaluations should report both properties together with the answer configuration.
authors: Shaoang Li, Yanhang Shi, Jian Li
bullets: Reasoning traces can improve accuracy while also causing models to repeat stale conclusions.
Across three model families on HotpotQA and MuSiQue, separate calls improved evidence-following over continuation by 29.9–60.6 points.
Removing traces reduced accuracy similarly in both configurations, showing that benefiting from a trace differs from deferring to it.
The trace’s final line provides most of its value; gold evidence is most helpful before reasoning is written.
Renewed reasoning corrected conflicts more often than verification instructions, while distractors weakened correction.
papers.selection_reason: Studies reasoning-trace and evidence-following behavior in LLMs under different answer configurations.
papers.title: When Reasoning Traces Conflict with Evidence: How Answer Configuration Shapes Evidence Following
papers.tldr: Separate answer calls follow updated evidence far more reliably than continuing a model’s prior reasoning trace when the two conflict.

papers.abstract: We study continual linear regression in a high-dimensional regime, where a learner observes a sequence of tasks and updates its parameters sequentially. In this setting, we derive an explicit closed-form expression for the generalization loss of a model trained with gradient descent for a fixed number of steps per task, which holds for arbitrary teachers. We prove that the optimal fixed step size decays nearly inversely with the number of tasks, specifically as $\ln T / T$, for a single teacher and, more generally, i.i.d. teachers. Under this scaling, we show that the resulting generalization loss is asymptotically equivalent to that achieved by optimally tuned L2 (isotropic) regularization. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to generalized ridge regression with diagonal regularization matrices, obtaining a closed-form characterization of the generalization loss and identifying necessary and sufficient conditions under which the optimal regularizer is isotropic. Finally, we identify a regime where the optimal step size remains finite even as the number of tasks tends to infinity, thus revealing a non-trivial tradeoff between task variability and implicit regularization, in contrast to the i.i.d. teacher scaling. Our theoretical predictions are corroborated by experiments on both linear models and neural networks, providing practical guidance for the design of continual learning systems.
authors: Gilad Karpel, Daniel Soudry
bullets: Provides a closed-form generalization-loss expression for fixed-step gradient descent across sequential tasks with arbitrary teachers.
For a single teacher or i.i.d. teachers, the optimal step size decreases nearly as ln(T)/T and matches optimally tuned isotropic L2 regularization asymptotically.
Characterizes generalization loss under diagonal generalized ridge regularization and gives conditions for when the optimal regularizer is isotropic.
Identifies a task-variability regime where the optimal step size remains finite as the number of tasks grows, unlike the i.i.d.-teacher case.
Experiments on linear models and neural networks support the theoretical predictions and offer guidance for continual-learning design.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of continual linear regression and regularization.
papers.title: Optimal Explicit and Implicit Regularization Strengths in High-Dimensional Continual Linear Regression
papers.tldr: The paper derives optimal implicit and explicit regularization strategies for high-dimensional continual linear regression, showing how step size should scale with task count and variability.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal agents have made significant progress in interacting with open worlds. However, their ability to self-evolve remains limited. Supervised fine-tuning enables imitation but not active experience organization, while outcome-based reinforcement learning promotes exploration yet underuses intermediate trajectory information. Therefore, we propose EvolvingBrain, which uses an adaptive skill system as the brain for agent self-evolution, consisting of two following components. Stratified Skill Self-Evolution: extracts Procedural Patterns and Problematic Patterns from model-specific trajectories, summarizes experience by generating skills, and evolves through multiple interactions with the open world, ultimately forming a Stratified Skill Architecture consisting of Domain, Plan, and Action/Trap Skills, which provides the agent with a multi-granularity knowledge repository and a novel evolution approach. State-Aware Adaptive Execution: summarizes long-horizon interactions into Structured Abstractive Memory and uses it to guide the State-Aware Skill Fusion Strategy, enabling the agent to utilize knowledge according to its current state. Experiments on VAB-Minecraft and DiscoveryWorld demonstrate that EvolvingBrain improves success rates on open-world tasks and exhibits generalization capabilities. Our code is provided in the supplementary materials and will be publicly released in the camera-ready version.
authors: Runxuan Liu, Jingqi Shi, Baoxin Wang, Honghong Zhao, Haoyuan Xu, Yueqing Sun, Jiafeng Liang, Tao He, Dayong Wu, Qi Gu, Shijin Wang, Ming Liu, Bing Qin
bullets: Addresses the limits of imitation learning and outcome-only reinforcement learning in organizing and exploiting intermediate experience.
Extracts procedural and problematic patterns from trajectories to generate skills through repeated world interactions.
Builds a stratified skill architecture with domain, plan, and action/trap skills for multi-granularity knowledge storage.
Uses structured abstractive memory and state-aware skill fusion to select and combine skills during long-horizon interactions.
Improves open-world task success rates and demonstrates generalization on VAB-Minecraft and DiscoveryWorld.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive skill system and structured memory for self-evolving agents in open worlds.
papers.title: EvolvingBrain: An Adaptive Skill System for Multi-modal Agents Self-Evolution in Open Worlds
papers.tldr: EvolvingBrain enables multimodal agents to self-evolve in open worlds by continually learning structured skills from experience and adapting their use to the current state.

papers.abstract: The closed world asks AI for specialized competence and lets it manufacture the iid data its theory assumes: a fixed criterion licenses collecting examples until the task is covered. The open world asks for versatility --- taking up tasks a machine was not built for, from few examples and with little prior from a human designer --- and offers data that is grouped, not shuffled. Its tasks are not known in advance, so a machine must do inference-time learning (1st requirement). Modeling tasks as sharing latent factors and decomposing the training objective, we derive two more: a *rich representation*, retaining more than iid generalization requires, and a predictive disentanglement that aligns inputs and outputs into matched low-dimensional groups. The analysis further predicts the need for a consistent inner learner, and the benefit of long contexts spanning related tasks. We test these claims on language models up to 8B, asking whether a model has a property (qualitative) rather than how much it wins (quantitative). Models that meet the requirements improve as data from related tasks accumulates; the rest degrade, and neither scale nor layer-type interleaving repairs this.
authors: Jianyu Zhang, L\'eon Bottou
bullets: Open-world settings involve unknown tasks, few examples, and grouped rather than iid data.
The analysis identifies three requirements: inference-time learning, representations richer than iid generalization needs, and aligned low-dimensional input–output groups.
A consistent inner learner and long contexts spanning related tasks are also predicted to help.
Experiments with language models up to 8B find that models meeting these requirements improve as related-task data accumulates, while others degrade.
Neither model scale nor interleaving different layer types fixes failures to meet the requirements.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses inference-time learning as a core requirement for open-world AI.
papers.title: Open-world AI: a Tale of Three Requirements
papers.tldr: Open-world AI requires inference-time learning, rich representations, and predictive disentanglement to improve across previously unseen related tasks.

papers.abstract: Image-to-text (I2T) understanding and text-to-image (T2I) generation are dual tasks in unified multimodal models (UMMs). Reconstructive post-training couples these tasks, but existing reconstruction-based methods remain perception-centric and provide limited supervision for reasoning about structure, intent, and transformation. We propose ReasonUni, a reasoning-augmented reconstructive post-training framework that extends this coupling beyond perception. Given an original image and an editing instruction, the UMM first reasons about what and how to edit and describes the target state, then generates the corresponding target image conditioned on this understanding output. To jointly optimize both modules, we introduce TreeGRPO, a tree-structured reinforcement learning method that samples multiple reasoning paths and candidate images per path, then aggregates visual rewards to update both modules under a unified objective. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate consistent gains in both understanding and generation, showing that reasoning-augmented reconstruction yields genuine mutual gains for UMMs.
authors: Feize Wu, Zhiyuan Yan, Yuhuan Hong, Yuwei Niu, Zongjian Li, Zheyuan Liu, Bin Lin, Jinbo Yan, Jie Qin, Xudong Mao, Limeng Qiao, Guanglu Wan, Li Yuan
bullets: Targets the limited structural, intentional, and transformational reasoning in reconstruction-based multimodal training.
Given an image and editing instruction, the model reasons about the edit, describes the target state, and generates the target image.
Introduces TreeGRPO, which samples multiple reasoning paths and candidate images and uses visual rewards to train both modules jointly.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks report consistent gains in both multimodal understanding and image generation.
The abstract does not specify numerical results, datasets, or detailed limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Reasoning-augmented reconstruction for unified multimodal understanding and generation models.
papers.title: ReasonUni: Reasoning-Augmented Reconstruction Advances Unified Multimodal Models
papers.tldr: ReasonUni improves unified multimodal models by adding explicit editing reasoning to image reconstruction and jointly optimizing reasoning and generation with tree-structured reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Automating organizational work means answering many small typed questions about one piece of state (does this email need a reply, how urgent is it, who owns it) with probabilities good enough to act on without a human. The open typed-decision model we compare against, like a standard cross-encoder, answers each question with a separate pass over the input. We present Verdict-MQ, an open encoder that reads a case once and answers all of its questions: given identical retained state tokens after truncation (verified on every reported case), a structured attention mask makes the state encoding independent of the questions, keeps questions from influencing each other, and makes option order irrelevant by construction. On the typed-decisions benchmark, a 395M Verdict-MQ matches the soft gold labels significantly better than the released 421M Laya specialist on all five fresh seeds (KL 0.080 vs 0.117, Brier 0.045 vs 0.061), an advantage that survives per-system temperature scaling; its higher accuracy (0.801 vs 0.767) lies past the benchmark's own saturation point, so we read that margin as closer agreement with the benchmark's labelling teacher. On RACE, BoolQ and MultiRC, against a matched fine-tuned baseline it wins on MultiRC and loses on RACE and on BoolQ, where its training is unstable; we measure zero-shot references ourselves, including a closed general system (Jev) that beats every fine-tuned encoder. A controlled comparison measures what the shared state costs: giving each question its own question-aware copy of the state gains 0.9-3.5 points on RACE and MultiRC at 1.4-2.5x the per-case latency, and nothing measurable on typed decisions, with the invariance guarantees unchanged.
authors: Avdhesh Singh Chouhan, Jack Perry
bullets: Structured attention makes state encoding independent of questions, prevents question interaction, and makes option order irrelevant.
On the typed-decisions benchmark, the 395M model beats the released 421M specialist on soft-label agreement and accuracy across five seeds.
Against a matched fine-tuned baseline, it wins on MultiRC but loses on RACE and BoolQ, where training is unstable.
Question-specific state copies improve RACE and MultiRC by 0.9–3.5 points at 1.4–2.5× latency, but show no measurable benefit on typed decisions.
The study also reports zero-shot references, including a closed general system that outperforms all fine-tuned encoders.
papers.selection_reason: Structured attention mask enables shared state encoding across many questions, reducing per-case latency.
papers.title: Verdict: Encode Once, Decide Many
papers.tldr: Verdict-MQ encodes each case once to answer many typed questions, improving typed-decision calibration and accuracy while trading some performance for lower repeated-processing cost on standard QA tasks.

papers.abstract: Calibrating a conformal prediction set at each early exit does not preserve coverage once a data-dependent exit is selected. We construct one terminal path score from prefix maxima, calibrate a single split-conformal quantile, and return nested prefix sets that all contain the valid terminal set. The guarantee is selection-safe without an alpha/L correction and holds simultaneously for every post-calibration label-free stopping policy that preserves terminal-set containment. We also bound the efficiency cost of the path maximum by the empirical tail of the early-over-terminal score excess. Across eight encoder task-backbone cells, pathwise selection attains macro coverage 0.901 versus 0.814 for naive layerwise selection, with average set size 1.41 and latency fraction 0.71. On CIFAR-100 with a 24-exit ViT-L/16 (n_cal=500), first-eligible stopping at budget b=4 attains coverage 0.902, set size 2.76, and latency fraction 0.57, and the same calibration supports deployment-time budget changes without refitting. In a joint exit-count/calibration-size sweep at n=100, pathwise set size moves only from 3.02 to 3.11 as exits increase from 4 to 24, while Bonferroni degenerates to the full label space for 12 or more exits. Paired comparison against MinSE valid selection at (n,L)=(100,24) gives a set-size difference of 0.80 [0.47, 1.13]. Full-vocabulary decoder experiments remain a negative boundary, with sets of 7,162-9,620 tokens. Pathwise calibration is most useful when candidate exits are many relative to calibration size, when budgets change after calibration, and when shallow heads return actionable sets.
authors: Adria Binte Habib, Ibne Farabi Shihab
bullets: Naive layerwise calibration loses coverage after data-dependent exit selection; pathwise calibration attains macro coverage 0.901 versus 0.814.
One split-conformal quantile yields nested prefix sets that contain the valid terminal set, supporting any post-calibration label-free stopping policy preserving containment.
Across eight task-backbone cells, average set size was 1.41 with latency fraction 0.71; on CIFAR-100, budget-4 stopping achieved coverage 0.902, set size 2.76, and latency fraction 0.57.
Pathwise calibration remained stable as exits increased from 4 to 24, while Bonferroni became degenerate at 12 or more exits; deployment budgets can change without refitting.
The approach is less effective for full-vocabulary decoding, producing sets of 7,162–9,620 tokens, and is most useful with many exits, limited calibration data, or actionable shallow-head sets.
papers.selection_reason: Conformal early-exit calibration for latency-efficient inference.
papers.title: Selection-Safe Conformal Early Exit: Distribution-Free Coverage under Adaptive Depth
papers.tldr: A prefix-max pathwise conformal score preserves distribution-free coverage under adaptive early-exit selection without alpha/L correction, while keeping prediction sets efficient across changing budgets.

papers.abstract: Can better feature discovery improve control over robot behavior through internal interventions and training data? Recent work in vision and language models reveals multidimensional features, motivating block-sparse featurizers (BSFs), which represent each feature in a low-dimensional subspace. We investigate whether recovering this structure provides an interpretable interface for steering vision-language-action models and shaping the data from which they learn. We show that BSFs recover several multi-dimensional task-relevant features underlying the model's computation (e.g., perception, language, proprioceptive state, episode phase, and control variables). We causally validate these features through fine-grained steering: targeted changes in visual perception, semantic representation, and spatial localization produce predictable changes in downstream action prediction. Finally, we use feature-based data attribution to isolate where a specific behavior (failure recovery) arises in the training dataset, identifying fewer than $1.4\%$ of training tokens whose masking is sufficient to remove the targeted behavior. Overall, our results show how matching featurizers to representation geometry can provide more effective tools for understanding and changing robot behavior.
authors: Aiden Swann, Mozes Jacobs, Mathilde Papillon, Siddharth Boppana, David Chanin, Dron Hazra, Usha Bhalla, Curt Tigges, Mac Schwager, Owen Lewis, Jack Merullo, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Atticus Geiger, Thomas Fel, Matthew Kowal
bullets: Recover task-relevant features spanning perception, language, proprioception, episode phase, and control variables.
Causal interventions show that steering visual, semantic, and spatial features predictably changes action predictions.
Feature-based data attribution traces failure-recovery behavior to fewer than 1.4% of training tokens.
Results support matching featurizers to representation geometry for more effective robot behavior analysis and modification.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates block-sparse featurizers in VLA models, with causal steering and feature-based data attribution for robot behavior.
papers.title: Multi-Dimensional Featurizers Yield Fine-Grained Steering and Data Shaping in Robot Foundation Models
papers.tldr: Block-sparse featurizers expose interpretable, multidimensional features in robot foundation models, enabling precise behavior steering and targeted training-data shaping.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are a promising approach to general purpose robot manipulation. While the internal computation of vision-language models, which compose the backbone of VLAs, has been studied extensively, less is known about how their perceptual and semantic representations are transformed into action in VLA models. We study this question mechanistically in three frontier VLA models ($\pi_{0.5}$, MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot) by analyzing the causal pathways through which the input image and the instruction shape actions. Across the three models, activation patching shows that causally relevant information influences the action expert (AE) through a narrow band of mid-to-late cross-attention layers, which we term the action-conditioning interface. The content of this information changes with token and layer within the model. Early-to-mid layer representations of the target noun token determine which object is selected, whereas mid-to-late layers carry the spatial information in text tokens that redirects the movement when patched. Where spatial information is stored in prompt tokens various based on the architecture. In MolmoAct2 the model forms task-conditioned representations at the text positions that follow the instruction, whereas $\pi_{0.5}$ additionally stores this information at image token positions. We show that these findings can be translated directly into improving model efficiency. We find that restricting MolmoBot's action expert conditioning to only 3 out of 36 layers reduces inference FLOPs by up to $33\%$ while maintaining comparable task success with the default model across 3,000 evaluation episodes ($46.7\%$ vs. $46.9\%$), and the same principle carries over to real-robot deployment of $\pi_{0.5}$.
authors: Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Mozes Jacobs, Siddharth Boppana, Tal Haklay, Eric Bigelow, Andrew Lee, Conor Watts, Thomas Icard, Mac Schwager, Owen Lewis, Jack Merullo, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Atticus Geiger, Thomas Fel, Matthew Kowal
bullets: Studies how perceptual and semantic representations become actions in three frontier VLA models: π₀.₅, MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot.
Activation patching identifies mid-to-late cross-attention layers as the main causal pathway into the action expert.
Early-to-mid representations of target nouns determine object selection, while later text representations encode spatial redirection.
Spatial information is stored differently across architectures, including instruction-following text positions and image-token positions.
Restricting MolmoBot conditioning to 3 of 36 layers cuts inference FLOPs by up to 33% while retaining comparable success; the approach also transfers to real-robot π₀.₅ deployment.
papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic causal analysis of vision-language-action robot models with efficiency gains, directly fitting embodied VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: Causal Analysis of Robot Foundation Models Enables Efficiency Gains
papers.tldr: Causal analysis reveals a narrow action-conditioning interface in VLA models, enabling substantial inference savings with comparable manipulation performance.

papers.abstract: Humans interpret multimodal observations of the world and forecast how it will evolve. Recent multimodal generative systems have demonstrated similar capabilities: they can integrate multimodal context and synthesize visual outputs that depict changes in the world. To characterize this emerging trajectory, we organize model capabilities into a four-level hierarchy and discover that higher-level tasks remain relatively underexplored despite model progress. To bridge this gap, we explore model performance on multi-step world state prediction, a high-level task that requires models to forecast successive future world states from multimodal observations and diverse references. Such a task requires models to possess entangled understanding and generation capabilities, as well as extensive world knowledge to translate human action sequences, physical transformations, and abstract visual reasoning into coherent visual outputs. We introduce WorldCast, a benchmark comprising 320 manually designed cases across eight categories, and evaluate 12 representative models. The conducted experiments yield three key insights: (a) advances in frontier models are rapidly pushing the boundaries of intelligent world modeling, with the GPT-Image-2.5 System scoring 72.8 and demonstrating early-stage visual state prediction capabilities on real-world tasks; (b) WorldCast reveals substantial gaps between models: even Nano Banana Pro reaches only 42.8 and the best open-source model scores 20.1, with deficits in handling complex context, entangled references, and reasoning-heavy tasks; (c) strong generative models effectively draw on the capabilities of their underlying language models. These findings highlight the need for multimodal generative models that are capable of dynamic planning and reasoning while also being deeply unified to faithfully simulate real-world states.
authors: Wenhao Yan, Haodong Li, Xiaotong Li, Yaxin Luo, Zhengrong Yue, Jialv Zou, Xu Huang, Haojin Yang, Nan Jia, Yan Feng, Peng Pei, Xunliang Cai
bullets: Organizes visual world-modeling capabilities into a four-level hierarchy and identifies high-level prediction as underexplored.
Introduces 320 manually designed cases across eight categories to evaluate multi-step world state prediction.
Evaluates 12 representative models, finding large performance differences and weaknesses in complex-context, reference-entangled, and reasoning-heavy tasks.
Reports early promising capabilities from frontier models, while open-source systems remain substantially behind.
Finds that strong visual generators benefit from the capabilities of their underlying language models.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and evaluation of multimodal generative models for multi-step world state prediction, directly relevant to world modeling.
papers.title: WorldCast: Exploring Intelligent Visual Generation in World State Prediction
papers.tldr: WorldCast benchmarks how well multimodal generative models can predict successive future world states from complex observations and references, revealing strong progress but major reasoning and planning gaps.

papers.abstract: Video generators serve as interactive worlds for exploration and simulation, yet realistic and visually appealing frames do not necessarily depict a consistent 3D world. Existing benchmarks assess selected geometric properties or use vision-language models to judge memory and consistency, leaving systematic 3D evaluation underexplored. We introduce Orbia, the first benchmark dedicated to a systematic and comprehensive evaluation of 3D consistency in interactive world models. Through controlled exploration and revisit, we organize the evaluation into three dimensions: input preservation, generated-content persistence, and 3D self-consistency. For input preservation, registered RGB-D references and annotated anchors support appearance, geometry, and spatial stability measurements.
